news.title: Disinformation videos, likely from Russia, are exploiting real people to malign Senate candidates
news.text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Social media videos believed to be produced with artificial intelligence and linked to Russia are misusing real people’s names and photographs to spread disinformation about two Democratic Senate candidates in the final stretch of midterm voting.

One of the targets is Sherrod Brown, who is running against Republican Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio. The video, which appears to include some AI manipulation, depicts a newscast and includes a picture of Haya Akbik, who interned for Brown several years ago. 

It was appalling to Akbik, who told The Associated Press that any claims attributed to her in the clip are “completely made up."

“It’s my name, it’s my reputation, making this allegation, and it’s just completely false,” she said. “And it harms the senator, someone else, in the process. So, it’s just messed up.”

The videos demonstrate how foreign adversaries continue to use a familiar playbook to try to influence American voters who are deciding which party controls Congress next year. The threat could be magnified with AI, a powerful tool for fabricating damaging information that can sometimes appear very real. 

Another target is James Talarico, who is running against Republican Ken Paxton for a Senate seat in Texas. The video, also believed to include some AI manipulation, is framed as a direct-to-camera confessional from a former student of Talarico.

“The most powerful people in the world know they can't beat James Talarico with the truth, so they're slandering him with AI deepfakes, foreign bots, and conspiracy theories to protect their broken, corrupt political system,” Talarico spokesperson JT Ennis said in a statement.

The social media company X has taken down the initial posts that shared the videos and suspended the users for violating the platform’s rules. However, copies could still be found online Tuesday — some with hundreds of shares — demonstrating how difficult it can be to contain disinformation that can proliferate in the final days of an election. 

Experts see a resemblance to Russian clips from 2024

The videos resemble clips from a Russian network known as Storm-1516 that targeted former Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris and her running mate, Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz, two years ago. 

The new ones bear similar hallmarks and are likely products of the same network, according to Clemson University professor and media forensics expert Darren Linvill. He found that the accounts that shared recent material had also shared former content from Storm-1516. 

The Russian Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In the past, it has denied interfering in U.S. elections. 

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which has publicly identified some videos as Russian disinformation in past election cycles, also didn't respond to a request for comment.

Hany Farid, a Dartmouth College professor who studies artificial intelligence deepfakes, said his analyses showed that videos targeting Brown and Talarico were likely either generated or manipulated using the technology.

He noted the video targeting Brown is a “fairly low-tech fake." The other one, targeting Talarico, is likely generated by AI and “it is consistent with previous disinformation campaigns released close to Election Day,” Farid said.

Akbik said the video featuring her shows the importance of Congress regulating “AI slop on the internet.”

“This is so damaging,” she said.

news.title: Kamala Harris and JD Vance's Popularity Compared as 2028 Rumors Swirl
news.text: As the midterm elections loom, speculation is growing over who could emerge as contenders in the 2028 presidential race. Polling has pointed to high-profile figures such as Vice President JD Vance and former Vice President Kamala Harris as potential frontrunners, as the field could begin to take shape in the coming weeks. The months after the midterms often bring the presidential field into clearer focus, as prospective candidates begin laying the groundwork for campaigns. Both Harris and Vance have been asked about potential runs, as have Democratic Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and California’s Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom. Even Donald Trump has been asked who he sees as a successor to MAGA. Harris lost her 2024 White House bid to Trump. Newsweek reached out to the White House to get comment from Vance and to Harris' office via email on Tuesday. What do the Polls Show A YouGov/Economist poll released on Tuesday shows Harris' favorability slightly ahead of Vance's. The current Vice President's total favorability is 41 percent versus a 53 percent unfavorable rating. Comparatively, Harris' total favorability is 43 percent compared to a 54 percent total unfavorable rating. The poll surveyed 1,440 U.S. registered voters from October 23–26, 2026, and has a margin of error of 3 percent. Craig Agranoff, political professor at Florida Atlantic University, told Newsweek on Tuesday that "the 2028 talk will ramp up the moment the midterm results are clear. That is the normal cycle. Candidates and donors start positioning the day after, especially if one party gains or loses ground. I do not take polling this far out as a serious forecast. Two years is a long time in politics. Name recognition drives most of these early numbers. A lot of voters have not even started thinking about 2028 yet." Agranoff continued: "The recent surveys show Vance with a clear lead on the Republican side and Harris ahead of a scattered Democratic field, but nearly half of Democrats still have no preference. That is useful for seeing who is known right now. It is a weak guide for what a candidate should expect if they jump in. Actual campaigns, debates, and primary turnout will rewrite the field long before 2028. Midterm outcomes will matter more than these early snapshots." A Harvard CAPS / Harris Poll last month shows Harris' favorability at 43 percent and her unfavorable rating at 46 percent. Vance's favorability in the poll was 41 percent versus a 44 percent unfavorable rating. The poll surveyed 2,200 registered voters from September 26-28, 2026, and had a margin of error of 2.1 percent. A Marquette Law School Poll earlier this year showed Harris' favorability at 37 percent compared to a 58 percent unfavorable rating and 5 percent had not heard enough. In the same poll, Vance landed a 39 percent favorability rating compared to a 54 percent unfavorable rating and 8 percent had not heard enough. That poll surveyed 1,001 adults across the country from May 20-26, 2026, and had a margin of error of 3.4 percent. Grant Davis Reeher, a professor of political science at Syracuse University, told Newsweek on Tuesday, "It’s still way, way too early to start concluding anything. We’ll have a slightly better idea after the results of the midterms come in, but even then that won’t say much about potential individual presidential candidates. The Democrats could win big and still damage their brand by dragging the country through another impeachment proceeding that leads nowhere, for instance. A more moderate Republican who is more open about the failures of Trump 2.0 could surface. Etc. "And I still maintain that Harris will not emerge as a top contender for the Democratic nomination once we get more into the season. This is still name recognition, combined with smaller sets of loyal voters. Unless the party has some kind of defeat wish. But you are right in that once the midterms are in the rear-view mirror, we will enter the presidential sweepstakes (to mix a metaphor)," Reeher concluded. Overall, on YouGov's website, Harris has a 49 percent popularity rating compared to 32 percent who dislike her and 16 percent who are neutral. Similarly, Vance's popularity score on the site is 38 percent compared to 45 percent who dislike him and 12 percent who are neutral. The site calculates its popularity score by taking the proportion of people who view something positively and expressing it as a percentage of all those who have given an opinion, YouGov says in part, including “have heard of”. That calculation is also used for neutral, heard of and negative scores, they add. YouGov notes that the data mirrors demographics across the country and is weighted "to be nationally representative." Meanwhile, a recent New York Times/Siena Research Institute poll showed both Harris and Vance leading their respective parties in potential 2028 primaries. Vance had 33 percent compared to Secretary of State Marco Rubio's 23 percent and 8 percent said Trump. For Democrats, Harris landed 12 percent, Newsom had 9 percent, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg had 7 percent and New York Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez had 6 percent. The poll surveyed 850 registered voters about the GOP primary and 1,170 registered voters about the Democratic primary from October 12-19, 2026, and had a margin of error of 1.9 percent. What Harris and Vance Have Said About a Potential 2028 Run Vance has repeatedly declined to formally commit to a 2028 presidential campaign, saying his focus is on serving in the current administration. "Yes, after the midterms, I will eventually have to make that decision," he told Megyn Kelly in June, in part, amid a wide-ranging interview. Speaking to CBS News Sunday Morning in June alongside second lady Usha Vance, JD said, in part, "I have no doubt that the president of the United States is going to be very supportive of anything that I ultimately decide to do." He added, "But we really just haven't talked about what that thing will be." In May, when asked about Trump’s previous comments calling a possible Vance-Rubio ticket a "dream team", Vance told Newsweek during a White House news conference that Americans would likely unfavorably view “someone who’s barely been in one office for a year and a half angling for a job two and a half years down the road,” adding, “There are few topics I want to talk about less.” He told CBS News this month that "of course" there is a chance that he doesn't run later, adding, "anything could happen." In April, Harris said that she was "thinking about it,” after being directly asked about any 2028 plans by Rev. Al Sharpton. She later told Sharpton that “I am thinking about it in the context of who and where and how can the best job be done for the American people,” Harris said. “That’s how I’m thinking about it. I’ll keep you posted.” She told CNN recently, “The American people want leaders who aren’t just occupied with looking in the mirror. They want leaders who are looking at the people, you know?” “And they can tell the difference.” “I go back and forth. I honestly go back and forth,” Harris also told the outlet regarding which way she’s leaning. “There’s so many factors.” Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: As the midterms are just one week away, speculation is growing over who could officially throw their hat into the 2028 race.
news.author: Anna Commander

news.title: Rep. Tom Tiffany claims Kamala Harris visit signals weakness in David Crowley’s Wisconsin campaign
news.text: Former Vice President Kamala Harris’ recent trip to Wisconsin to stump for Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Crowley shows his campaign is struggling to rally voters, according to his Republican opponent, Rep. Tom Tiffany. Harris arrived in the key battleground state on Monday to campaign alongside Crowley in Milwaukee, a visit coming just eight days before Election Day. "For the last year and a half, I know many of us have been going through a whole lot of emotion: anger, sadness, disappointment, destruction, depression, all kinds of emotions," Harris told supporters at Milwaukee’s Pfister Hotel. "And we've been feeling powerless. People have been feeling like ‘I can't do anything about this. ’ And I know how much pain people are in. I know how it is creating so much fear among so many communities of people." KAMALA HARRIS CALLS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION 'MOST CALLOUS AND CORRUPT' IN AMERICAN HISTORY Tiffany asserted that Harris was brought in to energize a Democratic base where Crowley’s campaign has lagged amid a sense of national political fatigue caused by polarization and endless campaign messaging. "This is clearly a move that says that they're struggling to get their base to vote. David Crowley has not excited the base," Tiffany told Fox News Digital. ABORTION, ICE AND SOCIALISM SPARK FIREWORKS IN SWING STATE GOVERNOR DEBATE: 5 TOP MOMENTS Critics and political opponents have accused Crowley of being handpicked by Democratic leaders, including Gov. Tony Evers, as a centrist alternative to more progressive candidates such as state Rep. Francesca Hong, whom Crowley narrowly defeated in the primary. The critique echoes challenges Harris faced during her own presidential bid. MEET THE DEMOCRAT WHO NARROWLY DEFEATED SOCIALIST RIVAL IN KEY SWING-STATE BATTLE OVER THE PARTY’S FUTURE "It was, once again, the Democrats that pulled somebody off the bench," Tiffany said. "They hand-picked them rather than letting democracy work in their own party, and there's people very frustrated with that. They're trying to excite their base, and it's a problem for them. " Tiffany has framed himself as a common-sense candidate while targeting Crowley, the current Milwaukee County Executive, over local economic conditions. "It's not in his DNA to reduce costs for people in Wisconsin or to reduce taxes," Tiffany said. "He is going to raise taxes. That's what he's done every single year when he's been county executive. That's not what people want to hear. " A spokesperson for Crowley's campaign pushed back in a statement to Fox News Digital, highlighting his efforts to detail his affordability plans amid inflation, blaming Tiffany and the Trump administration. "David Crowley is criss-crossing the state to discuss his plan to lower costs for working families who are struggling to pay their bills because of Congressman Tom Tiffany and Donald Trump’s unaffordable MAGA agenda," the spokesperson said. "David has spent his career lowering costs for working families including balancing the budget and lowering the property tax rate every single year as County Executive." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Meanwhile, Tom Tiffany went to Washington and sold out working Wisconsinites to give the same billionaires funding his campaign massive tax breaks," the statement continued.
news.summary: Tom Tiffany says Kamala Harris' Milwaukee rally for David Crowley reveals Democrats are struggling to energize their base before Wisconsin's election.

news.title: Hackers Targeted Fec Website, Officer Says, Disrupting Spending Filings a Week Before US Elections
news.text: An FEC officer reported an attempted breach of agency systems as electronic spending filings were disrupted a week before the 3 November US elections, according to an email seen by Reuters. The interruption blocked mandatory reports detailing political spending on specific races.Campaign finance officers had been unable to submit required reports late on Monday before the Federal Election Commission posted an outage notice. The agency tracks spending by candidates and political committees, with disclosure taking on particular importance during the final days of congressional races.The elections will determine whether President Donald Trump's Republicans retain their majorities in Congress for the next two years. The FEC does not administer US elections, and the outage should have no effect on voters' ability to cast ballots.FEC Website Officer Describes Breach AttemptAn FEC electronic filings officer described the reason for the shutdown in an email to several campaign compliance firms on Monday night, according to Reuters.'We have a bad actor attempting to breach FEC systems. As a result, we've had to temporarily shut down our web facing services,' the officer wrote.The FEC's public statement confirmed the interruption without providing further details about its cause. The agency stated, 'at this time, the FEC's electronic filing system is currently offline and our IT staff are actively working to restore service.'The agency confirmed that users could still search its website for past reports and declined further comment on the outage. Its status notice placed the beginning of the interruption at around 10 p.m. ET on Monday, or 0200 GMT on Tuesday.The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency referred questions to the FEC. The FBI did not immediately return messages seeking comment, Reuters reported.FEC Website Outage Restricts Spending DisclosureThe interruption prevents organisations from submitting the FEC's 24-hour and 48-hour spending reports, which detail expenditure on specific races. Previously filed reports remain searchable, but the missing submissions restrict access to newer spending information.Steven Mele, president and CEO of political finance compliance firm MBA Consulting Group, described the disruption in comments reported by Reuters.'I've never seen this in 26 years,' he stated. 'The result is there will be less disclosure on the elections' until the system is restored.The timing matters because super PACs and dark money groups are spending heavily as the races approach their final days. Super PACs can accept unlimited contributions from wealthy individuals and corporations and spend on campaigns with few restrictions.FEC Website Disruption Coincides With Record SpendingPolitical advertising tracker AdImpact put spending on advertising and future reservations at roughly $11.21 billion (£8.4 billion), describing the midterms as the most expensive US election in history. Its comparison was with $11.2 billion (£8.4 billion) spent across all races in 2024, including $3.2 billion (£2.4 billion) on the presidential contest between Trump and former Vice President Kamala Harris.Brendan Glavin, research director at nonpartisan campaign watchdog OpenSecrets, reported average spending of more than $50 million (£37.5 million) a day by super PACs and dark money groups over the preceding week. More than $250 million (£187.4 million) was reported on 20 October alone, he added.'These are the key reports that tell us what is happening,' Glavin stated. 'In the last days of the election this is the only way for us to keep track of where the money's being spent' and who is spending it.
news.author: Aries Señara

news.title: Trump plans to loosen restrictions on methane emissions from oil drilling
news.text: President Donald Trump is expected to announce plans Tuesday to loosen a Biden-era rule that aimed to reduce planet-warming emissions of methane from oil and gas drilling.Trump was to deliver the announcement as he campaigned in Texas, according to an administration official speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak on the record ahead of the official announcement.The move aims to encourage more domestic drilling as Trump faces criticism over high fuel prices amid the U.S. war in Iran. Methane is responsible for about a third of planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions, scientists estimate.Cuts in methane emissions have emerged in recent years as a global priority to slow the rate of climate change. Oil and gas operations are the largest industrial source of methane, which is the main component in natural gas and far more potent to the atmosphere than carbon dioxide in the short term.The invisible gas leaks from equipment and is sometimes released into the atmosphere by oil drillers or burned off as a waste byproduct during crude production.RELATED STORY | UN report calls out US emissions, says world can no longer avoid overshooting key climate targetEnvironmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin previewed the changes last month, saying they would eliminate the agency’s “Super Emitter Program” that requires companies to investigate and repair major methane releases from oil and natural gas facilities. The agency would also set less restrictive standards for small oil and gas wells.The loosening of the emissions rule comes as Trump and Republicans in Congress have been methodically dismantling climate policies enacted under former President Joe Biden. That's included the revocation of a scientific finding that was central to U.S. action on greenhouse gas emissions, lower fuel economy standards for vehicles and a move to repeal emission restrictions for coal and natural gas power plants.Environmental groups criticized the latest rollback.“It will impose a heavier pollution burden on our front-line communities and make our energy sector less efficient,” said Max Lopez, an Environmental Law & Policy Center attorney.Zeldin has said the methane rule would have cost $18 billion and was holding back the U.S. energy industry.“The Trump EPA is committed to fixing this so the U.S. can reach its full energy potential,” he said last month.The Biden methane rule was announced by officials including former Vice President Kamala Harris during a 2023 U.N. climate conference in the United Arab Emirates. Federal officials under Biden said it would prevent an estimated 58 million tons (52.6 million metric tonnes) of methane emissions by 2038.IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | El Niño is expected to shape this winter’s weather, and it could hit your budget tooWhile previous EPA regulations focused only on new oil and gas wells in the U.S., the Biden rule regulated existing wells. Operators also would have needed to plug leaking methane from smaller wells that produce just 6% of the nation’s oil and gas while accounting for up to half of all methane emissions from oil and gas fields.The final rule was published in 2024 but never went into effect. The EPA last year imposed an 18-month delay to give companies time to meet new inspection requirements and other provisions.The rule was crafted to be coordinated with a methane fee, approved in the 2022 climate law. The fee program would have levied a “waste emissions charge” of as much as $1,500 per metric ton of methane on energy producers that exceed a certain level of methane emissions.The fee marked the first time the U.S. government directly imposed a fee, or tax, on greenhouse gas emissions. Congress repealed it weeks after Trump took office.
news.summary: President Donald Trump is expected to announce plans Tuesday to loosen a Biden-era rule that aimed to reduce planet-warming emissions of methane from oil and gas drilling.
news.author: AP via Scripps News Group

news.title: Susan Collins vs. Troy Jackson: Candidates' Final Appeal to Voters Compared
news.text: Republican Senator Susan Collins and her Democratic challenger Troy Jackson are making their final pitches to voters in Maine's U.S. Senate race, a critical battleground that could determine the balance of power in the upper chamber, as a new poll pointed to a tight race in the Pine Tree State. Maine has emerged as one of the most competitive Senate races of the 2026 midterm elections. Collins is an anomaly in the Senate, as she’s the only Republican representing a state that rejected President Donald Trump in all three of his presidential bids. Although she’s benefited from her personal popularity and bipartisan image in the past, Democrats believe she is more vulnerable than ever this year as Trump’s declining national approval rating weakens Republicans across the country. The competitive nature of the race was reflected in a new Marist University poll released Tuesday, giving Jackson a 2-point lead over Collins, 49 percent to 47 percent, among likely voters. It was conducted from October 22 to 25 among 1,449 registered voters, and had a margin of error of plus or minus 6.6 percentage points. Newsweek reached out to the Collins and Jackson campaigns for comment via email. Susan Collins and Troy Jackson's Message to Voters 1 Week to Midterm With one week until Election Day, both candidates have been traversing the state to make their case to voters. Collins wrote in a post to X that she was in Springvale, a village in Sanford, a city of nearly 23,000 residents that voted for Trump in 2024 after backing former President Joe Biden in 2020. “Great to meet the team at Moody’s Collision Center today in Springvale. Moody’s provides reliable service to customers across southern Maine and, as an employee-owned business, it invests in those who work there. Thanks for all you do to keep Mainers moving!” Collins wrote. Jackson, meanwhile, was set to appear at an event in Freeport, a Democratic-leaning coastal town known as the home of L.L. Bean, alongside gubernatorial candidate Hannah Pingree, Representative Chellie Pingree and Arizona Senator Mark Kelly, according to his campaign site. Both candidates have also unveiled new advertisements in the final stretch of the campaign. Jackson, in a new ad, said that Mainers will “decide the direction of this whole country.” “Is it for the billionaires and Trump, or everyday people like us? We can protect Social Security, get people healthcare, and keep more of what we earn. It won’t be easy, but I’ve learned that if your heart is in the right place, you can make things better,” he said. He added that he owes “nothing” to billionaires or Trump, but “everything to the people of Maine.” Collins, meanwhile, released a new ad featuring famed Maine broadcaster Bill Green, who questioned when Maine politics went “into the gutter,” lamenting the development as “shameful.” “Susan Collins is one of the most decent and honest people I know,” he said. “Now, I also know Troy Jackson. But we're not talking about buying a cord of wood here. We're sending someone to the US Senate, and Troy doesn't have the tools he needs to be effective.” Green appeared to be referring to Jackson’s background as a logger before his foray into politics. He said that both sides know Collins delivers for Maine and that she is “America’s most independent senator.” The ad drew backlash from Democrats, who criticized the comment about “buying a cord of wood.” Jordan Wood, a former Democratic congressional and Senate candidate, wrote in a post to X that the ad was “despicable” and made his “jaw drop.” Jackson addressed the ad in a video posted to X, calling it “out of touch.” “I know that people like you and Senator Collins talk down to people like me, but this is about a cord of wood. It’s about an economy that Susan Collins has created that people can’t afford to heat their homes,” he said. Susan Collins vs. Troy Jackson: Latest Polls in Maine Senate Race Polling has shown a tight race as Democrats hope the national environment will carry them to victory in Maine, a state that backed former Vice President Kamala Harris by about 7 points in the 2024 election. A Suffolk University poll gave Jackson a 2-point lead, 49 percent to 47 percent. It surveyed 500 Maine voters October 8-11 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.4 percentage points. Collins also trailed by 2 points in an InsiderAdvantage survey of 1,200 likely voters on October 13 and 14. Jackson’s support stood at 49 percent to 47 percent for Collins. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.83 percentage points. Jackson was up 4 points among 800 likely voters in a poll from The Washington Post and George Mason University, conducted from September 30 to October 5. Fifty percent said they planned to vote for Jackson, compared with 46 percent for Collins. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.6 percentage points. Polls underestimated Collins in her 2020 reelection bid. She trailed Democrat Sara Gideon in public surveys but won with more than 50 percent of the vote. Forecasters like the Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball classified the race as a toss-up. Jackson had an edge in prediction markets as of Tuesday, when his chances of victory stood at 62 percent on Kalshi and 63 percent on Polymarket. Prediction markets allow traders to buy and sell contracts tied to political outcomes and current events, aggregating real‑money wagers into probability estimates. Prices fluctuate as traders react to polling, fundraising, candidate developments and broader political trends. They measure trader sentiment at a given moment but do not always accurately predict the future. Latest Developments in Maine Senate Race Collins and Jackson faced off in four debates earlier in October in hopes of winning over undecided voters, who could be critical to the outcome of the race. During the debate, they discussed issues including data centers, the economy and Trump. In one viral moment, the final debate was briefly interrupted by a data center protester as Collins was speaking, about which she said: “This is obviously one of Troy’s supporters.” Jackson responded: “Oh, shut up. I don’t even know that kid.” Jackson’s remark drew some criticism from Collins. Jackson declined to apologize during an interview on CNN’s State of the Union. “I’ve had four debates with Senator Collins," he said. "I’ve shook her hand afterwards every time. What I’m not going to be is talked down to by Senator Collins, I’m not going to be accused of things like that. I’m fighting for Mainers and I just think that was another situation where she was talking down to me, so I’m not going to apologize for that.” Jackson outraised Collins 4-to-1 in the most recent quarter, though he remains behind in overall fundraising and outside assistance. Last week, Collins announced that the Trump administration agreed to release 315,000 barrels of home heating oil from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve, which could help Mainers ahead of the winter, as about half the state relies on oil to heat their homes. Early Voting Underway in Maine In-person absentee voting began on October 5 and will continue until Thursday. Polling locations are open from 6 a.m. or 10 a.m. to 8 p.m., depending on a town’s population. As of Monday, 251,036 absentee ballots had been requested and 197,104 had been returned and accepted, according to data from Maine's secretary of state office. news.summary: Maine's U.S. Senate race could determine the balance of power in the upper chamber after the midterms.

Miranda Devine: Thanks very much, Guy. Good to be with you.

Guy Benson: I’ve been maybe a little surprised to see–not by the underlying sentiment, but the brazenness–that we’re seeing in some lefty circles about this hunger, this eagerness to get back to weaponizing political power against opponents quite openly and criminalizing politics. If Donald Trump loses the House and Senate, I would be worried if I were him, no matter how rich he is. news.title: Kamala Harris' phone calls that have 'repulsed' top Democrats: Party leaders and donors in 'panic mode' as her secret 2028 comeback plot is laid bare
news.text:
Michigan Democratic Senator Elissa Slotkin was emphatic.

'No,' she repeated when asked if Vice President Kamala Harris, and two-time failed presidential candidate, should seek higher office again.

Slotkin's answer to a worried 22-year-old University of Chicago student sparked a firestorm in the Democratic Party.

'It's funny, but it's not that funny,' the exasperated voter asked, pointing to Harris's lingering popularity among Democratic voters. 'Who's going to tell her no?'

'Someone has to tell Kamala Harris not to run.'

Slotkin conceded that Harris was not the 'fresh face' that the party needed.

It was a rare honest public moment of the party conversation about what to do with Harris as she steps up her activity on the campaign trail. 

Harris's catastrophic 15-week run for president in 2024 ended in her receiving some 6 million fewer popular votes than Biden won in 2020, just 226 electoral college votes to Donald Trump's 312, and the Democrats shedding support among loyal black and Hispanic voters. 

Any good will the Democrats expect to generate from a comeback in the midterms next week could be undermined by a failure to put forward a serious presidential candidate for 2028.

But telling Harris 'no' only serves as rocket fuel for her political motivations, Democratic sources familiar with her thinking told the Daily Mail.

Harris has long urged her supporters, 'don't let anyone tell you no,' citing a long list of people who told her that 'it was not her time' when she wanted to run for office.

'I eat no for breakfast,' she finishes, often with peals of laughter to signal her disdain for critics and doubters.

One Democratic insider told the Daily Mail that many Democratic donors and party officials are in 'panic mode' and looking for ways to end another Harris presidential campaign before it begins.

Harris supporters were not surprised when anonymous Democrats told the Wall Street Journal that Harris's husband Doug Emhoff had told them that he preferred that she not run.

Harris snapped back, sneering at those 'who think that I should just sit at home and eat bonbons and cook Doug's favorite foods,' reminding her critics in a CNN interview on Sunday that she could do both.

'I could cook Doug's favorite foods and do this,' she added.

Although Emhoff has been absent on the midterms campaign trail, he recently appeared with Harris in New Hampshire, again playing the role of a supportive spouse. 

Harris has long felt that she belongs in the Oval Office and that her failed 2024 campaign was not her fault, sources who worked with her told the Daily Mail.

The premise of her memoir 107 Days was that if she just had more time to campaign as the Democratic nominee, she would have defeated Donald Trump to become the president of the United States today.

Harris has been making calls to reconnect with donors, one Democratic strategist told the Daily Mail, and while they are polite, they are not always well received. 

'You don't want to say no to the former vice president,' one source familiar with the calls told the Daily Mail. 'At the same time, they are not committing to support her right now.' 

Many donors are still angry about how the Harris team spent over a billion dollars during the 2024 campaign, and there is little interest in supporting another campaign. 

When they hang up, the verdict is not kind to the former vice president. 

'They are repulsed and flabbergasted that she just won't take a hint,' another source familiar with Harris's conversations with some of the Democratic party's top donors told the Daily Mail.

Behind the scenes, donors are 'very snarky and condescending' about her chances. 

Other donors feel like Harris took too much time off, another source said, and was late to call them to process the results of her losing 2024 campaign. 

Harris is working to make up lost time, sources say, knowing that California Governor Gavin Newsom has also been courting their support. 

'Harris and Newsom have the same donors,' Lindy Li, a former Democratic fundraiser and author of the book, Unburdened, told the Daily Mail. 'That's why she's doing this, to basically mark her territory before it's too late. It's like a blood feud.'

LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman, who donated $17 million to Harris's presidential campaign in 2024, warned her in an interview that she faced a 'very challenging path' if she ran again. 

Harris, however, is pushing forward despite significant political headwinds. 

Last week, Harris very much looked like a candidate for office as she traveled across the country.

The failed presidential candidate, who turned 62 on Tuesday, campaigned for Democrats in Nevada, Mississippi and New Hampshire, with plans to go to Wisconsin and Georgia.

She's also doing more media appearances. 

'I'll be very specific. If I run, my motivation is not to beat other Democrats, it's to actually do the job,' she told CNN in an interview, revealing she was going 'back and forth' while mulling the decision. 

Behind the scenes, her allies are sharing a list of about two dozen top campaign aides and consultants she is working with as she mulls her decision, to prove to donors that she is serious about running again.

'She's serious about another run, but even if she ultimately decides against it, you want to have your team in place,' one former Harris campaign advisor told the Daily Mail.

Her behind-the-scenes activity is sparking a strong reaction from donors, who are fretting about how she would affect the race.

Right now, opposition to Harris is falling into two political camps, according to sources.

One camp believes that Democrats have to work to isolate the former vice president and stop her from running again, arguing that they made a mistake with Biden by trusting he would make the right decision until it was too late.

The second camp believes that Harris should be left alone to fail or succeed on her own steam, knowing that eventually she would lose interest or burn out if she tried to run again.

Supporters are sharing polls showing that Harris leads Vice President JD Vance by as much as five points compared to other top-tier Democrats like California Governor Gavin Newsom and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg – who only lead by one point. Vance is also leading New York Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez by five points in hypothetical matchups.

But the overall majority of top political figures in the party are downplaying her chances of success if she runs again.

The coolness from Democrats, donors and strategists and even outright hostility to Harris running again could actually work in her favor, one former Kamala Harris official told the Daily Mail.

'If there are people who disagree with you and are fighting with you about what you want, that makes your objective even more authentic,' Jamal Simmons, a former communications director for Harris, told the Daily Mail.

On the campaign trail and in interviews, she makes it abundantly clear that she has shed the cautious Biden-era politics of the past.

She wants to expand the Supreme Court, endorse statehood for Washington, DC, and Puerto Rico, and even signaled support for reforming the Electoral College.

Simmons, who left Harris's office after a year in the position, said that Harris should continue her public outreach and talk to as many people as possible about what went wrong in 2024 and grapple with 'uncomfortable truths' about the race.

'She should certainly talk to as many people as she can and secure as much support as possible if she wants to run,' he said.

Simmons cautioned that donors would grow impatient if she took too much time to make a decision.

'She's going to have to make a choice by Valentine's Day, out of fairness to everyone else,' he said. 'Leaving those people in limbo isn't fair.'

Democratic strategists told the Daily Mail that she needed to get out of her comfort zone and speak publicly about her ambitions if she wanted to be taken seriously.

'I think Kamala Harris can do anything she sets her mind to; she's just got to decide,' Simmons said.

The Daily Mail reached out to a representative for Harris for comment.

news.title: Trump plans to loosen restrictions on methane emissions from oil drilling
news.text:
President Donald Trump is expected to announce plans Tuesday to loosen a Biden-era rule that aimed to reduce planet-warming emissions of methane from oil and gas drilling.

Trump was to deliver the announcement as he campaigned in Texas, according to an administration official speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak on the record ahead of the official announcement.

The move aims to encourage more domestic drilling as Trump faces criticism over high fuel prices amid the U.S. war in Iran.

Cuts in methane emissions have emerged in recent years as a global priority to slow the rate of climate change. Oil and gas operations are the largest industrial source of methane, which is the main component in natural gas and far more potent to the atmosphere than carbon dioxide in the short term.

The invisible gas leaks from equipment and is sometimes released into the atmosphere by oil drillers or burned off as a waste byproduct during crude production.

The loosening of the emissions rule comes as Trump and Republicans in Congress have been methodically dismantling climate policies enacted under former President Joe Biden. That's included the revocation of a scientific finding that was central to U.S. action on greenhouse gas emissions, lower fuel economy standards for vehicles and a move to repeal emission restrictions for coal and natural gas power plants.

The Biden methane rule was announced by officials including former Vice President Kamala Harris during a 2023 U.N. climate conference in the United Arab Emirates. Federal officials under Biden said it would prevent an estimated 58 million tons (52.6 million metric tonnes) of methane emissions by 2038. 

The final rule was published in 2024 but never went into effect. The Environmental Protection Agency last year imposed an 18-month delay to give companies time to meet new inspection requirements and other provisions.

The rule was crafted to be coordinated with a methane fee, approved in the 2022 climate law. The fee program would have levied a “waste emissions charge” of as much as $1,500 per metric ton of methane on energy producers that exceed a certain level of methane emissions.

The fee marked the first time the U.S. government directly imposed a fee, or tax, on greenhouse gas emissions. Congress repealed it weeks after Trump took office.

Gruver reported from Fort Collins, Colorado.
news.summary: President Donald Trump is expected to announce plans to loosen a Biden-era rule that aimed to reduce planet-warming emissions of methane from oil and gas drilling

news.title: The Logic Behind Trump's 'Pretend I'm on the Ballot' Appeal
news.text:
In the 2024 presidential election, President Donald Trump won each of Iowa's four congressional districts. He won the 1st District by 8 points, the 2nd District by 10 points, the 3rd District (which includes Des Moines) by 4 points, and the 4th District, in the far western part of the state, by a landslide 31 points.

That — the place where he won by 31 points — is where Trump went last week, flying from Washington, D.C., nearly three hours each way to hold a rally in Sioux City for Rep. Ashley Hinson, the Republican who is in a close race for the Senate, and Zach Lahn, the Republican who is in a close race for governor.

Which raised the question: Why go to the place where Republicans are guaranteed a solid win? Why not campaign in a part of Iowa where the GOP needs help, needs to improve its performance?

The answer is low-propensity voters. There are a lot of Republican-leaning voters in the 4th District of Iowa who don't go to the polls for every election, but turned out in 2024 to vote for Trump. They are the kind who probably wouldn't turn out for a midterm election in 2026 with no Trump on the ballot. The GOP challenge is how to get their votes this time.

"MAGA low-propensity voters are a sizable part of our low-propensity voters," Jeff Kaufmann, the longtime chairman of the Iowa Republican Party, told me. "There is no way to turn them out without Trump himself. They don't get out to vote when Trump is not on the ballot."

Kaufmann asked the president to visit those voters where they live. "I said to the president, there is no mailer, no commercial, that can turn out the MAGA portion of our low-propensity voters," Kaufmann recalled. Only Trump in person.

Iowa Republicans know this because appealing to low-propensity voters is how they've won elections before. "They literally carried our current governor [Republican Kim Reynolds] over the line," Kaufmann said. "She will tell you that her reelection was because of the 4th District. We don't win statewide races, not just governor and Senate but attorney general and state auditor, without turnout in the 4th District -- especially during a midterm."

It's not just in Iowa. Last Friday, Trump traveled to Fort Myers, Florida, in a district he won by 31 points. On Saturday, he traveled to Perry, Georgia, in a district he also won by 31 points. And on Sunday, he traveled to Port Huron, Michigan, in a district he won by 32 points.

It's not that Republicans are in trouble in those places. Far from it. It's that Trump is aggressively trying to attract the voters who only come out when he is on the ballot — by asking them to vote like he is.

Trump has been widely mocked for asking voters to "pretend I'm on the ballot." The New Yorker said it shows that "only one subject truly animates Donald Trump on the campaign trail, and it is, of course ... himself." The Daily Beast called it a "desperate plea." And at his rally in Detroit Saturday with former President Barack Obama, Michigan Democrat Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed ridiculed Trump's visit to Port Huron and sarcastically asked voters, "Please make sure to vote like Donald Trump is on the ballot."

Despite what he said, it's probably safe to assume that El-Sayed does not really want the 9th Congressional District of Michigan, which includes Port Huron, to vote like Trump is on the ballot, since voters there gave the president that 32-point victory in 2024.

There is research showing that a low-propensity voter strategy makes sense in a lot of places. A 2025 report from Pew Research found that nationwide, voters who were eligible to vote in 2020 and 2022 but did not vote, and then did vote in 2024 — those voters leaned strongly to Trump. He won the 2024-only voters by 55 percent to Kamala Harris's 41 percent. And this was not just a tiny group of people. Pew found that 2024-only voters made up 12 percent of the entire electorate in the presidential race that year. It made a big difference for Trump.

Now the president is trying to do the same thing in the context of a midterm election. And if Republicans are trying to turn out low-propensity voters, it makes sense to ask them to pretend that Trump is on the ballot. It might not work, or it might not work everywhere. But it is probably the Republican Party's best shot at the moment. Speaking the day after the Sioux City rally, Jeff Kaufmann said, "I think we accomplished our goal, which was to energize turnout in the 4th District."

This content originally appeared on the Washington Examiner at https://www.washingtonexaminer.com/daily-memo/4779308/logic-behind-trump-pretend-im-on-ballot-appeal/.

news.title: Trump’s Attempt to the Tilt the Midterms Is Working—Against Republicans
news.text:
Donald Trump’s schemes are rarely the best-laid plans, but they often go awry all the same. So far, that’s what appears to be happening to the president’s most visible efforts to tilt next week’s midterm elections toward Republicans. His nationwide gerrymandering campaign and attacks on mail voting are threatening to backfire in key states, even as his attempts to pressure election officials fall short in court. It doesn’t mean we’re out of the woods, but it’s a reminder that presidents—even ones bent on exploiting their offices for political advantage—have only limited power to escape accountability for their failures.

I thought gerrymandering was a pretty foolproof way to give one party a leg up. How did Trump screw it up?

Let’s be clear about one thing from the jump: Nationwide, Trump’s gerrymandering push will probably still help his party hang on to House seats—just fewer than he initially thought. That’s because gerrymandering can backfire when pushed too far. Picture two congressional districts in Texas, which redrew its maps last year at Trump’s behest. In 2024, Trump won one of the districts by about 5 points; Kamala Harris won the other by more than 30. To make both districts more Republican-friendly, the Texas Legislature stretched their boundaries such that Trump would’ve won each by about 10 points—a big enough advantage to help Republican House candidates win in most years, but small enough for a wave election to swamp.

In fact, these examples are quite real. They describe Texas’ 34th and 35th Congressional Districts, which encompass heavily Hispanic areas that swung toward Trump in 2024. Except inflation, the war in Iran, and aggressive Immigration and Customs Enforcement actions have soured many Latinos on Trump, giving Democrats an opening. In the redrawn 34th District, Democratic Rep. Vicente Gonzalez sounds confident that he’ll win reelection. In the 35th, polls show Johnny Garcia, a Democratic former sheriff’s deputy, competitive with his GOP opponent. If both Democrats win, the redrawn maps will constitute what political observers call a “dummymander.” Redistricting on the assumption that Latinos would continue to vote as Republican as they did in 2024 may also come back to haunt Republicans in Florida, where polls suggest that Democrats could win some districts the GOP redrew this year to advantage themselves.

OK, what else isn’t going Trump’s way?

His attacks on mail voting, for one. The Supreme Court blocked an executive order that would have restricted mail voting, but the president’s cuts to the Postal Service—implemented under Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency—are causing other problems. ProPublica reports that during this year’s primary elections, service reductions increased the rejection rate for late-arriving mail ballots in rural parts of Washington, California, Oregon, and two states with critical Senate elections this year: North Carolina and Ohio. Rural voters overwhelmingly support Republicans, so Trump’s antipathy toward mail voting threatens to undermine his own party’s candidates in the general election too.

How about all the lawsuits Trump is filing? 

They haven’t been going well either. On Monday, a federal appeals court rejected the administration’s effort to force California to segregate thousands of mail ballots, which the government dubiously claims went to noncitizens. A judge in Alaska, meanwhile, sounds mighty skeptical of the Justice Department’s attempt to block certification of that state’s competitive Senate race if the Republican incumbent narrowly loses. And as the New Yorker reported this week, Republican and Democratic election officials have successfully resisted federal pressure to purge voter rolls of supposed nonvoters.

So can we mark our elections safe from Trump?

Not necessarily. Even if Republican dummymanders backfire next week, they might work as intended in less Democratic years. It’s also probable that we haven’t seen the extent of Trump’s attempts to meddle with the vote. He’s preemptively claiming that certain Republicans can lose only if Democrats “cheat,” which means lawsuits contesting the results are likely. As the New York Times reported today, state officials are bracing for a range of efforts to interfere, from federal officials seizing ballots to ICE raiding polling places. As the aftermath of the 2020 election proved, even Trump’s failed maneuvers can drive down public faith in the results and spark violence. Malevolence tempered by incompetence is still malevolence.

The most titillating midterms coverage: What if the election were sexy instead of nauseating? “Maybe during these midterms,” Scaachi Koul writes, “the Democrats are learning how much reward can come from letting a hot guy run his delicious little mouth.” Scaachi argues that after a decade of Trump, what the left needs most is a daddy. Lucky for us, she knows exactly who it should be.

A twisted romance: What if, at its core, You Can See Everything is a love story? Sam Adams makes the case that Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary is about something more tender than just matters of truth and reality.

Your burning questions, answered: In the special segment Decoder Rings Back, host Willa Paskin answers listeners’ queries about cultural mysteries. In this episode, Willa investigates why stores lock everything up now—and whether there’s really a shoplifting epidemic.

What’s a three-letter word for “where the door didn’t hit Kristi Noem on the way out”? (Hint: Christina Cauterucci covered this.) Solve these clues and more in today’s puzzle.

Enjoy your night and see you tomorrow!

news.title: Delaware Admits Glock Doesn’t Make Illegal Switches — But Sues Them Anyway
news.text:
Delaware sued Glock Thursday claiming the company failed to take measures to prevent criminals from illegally adding a component that enable the company’s guns to fire in fully-automatic, but conceded the company didn’t make illegal switches.

Several states have targeted the company’s popular semiautomatic pistols, either trying to prohibit future sales of the handgun or suing the company, claiming that it is too easy to convert the ubiquitous guns into fully-automatic firearms. Democratic Delaware Attorney General Kathy Jennings accused the company of being “neutrals” in efforts to prevent “gun violence” in a Thursday release that ignored the admission in the complaint that the manufacturer of the immensely popular pistols did not manufacture the illicit devices. “Our communities, and communities across America, are being terrorized by weapons with destructive power never intended or legal for civilian use,” Jennings claimed in a statement in the release. “Glock knew. They could have acted. They chose profit over people.”

In the 82-page complaint, Delaware conceded that the devices were not manufactured by Glock and that third parties were responsible for the illegal distribution and production of the so-called “Glock switches,” some of which had the company’s logo on them without the company’s authorization.

“While Glock itself does not produce these deadly items, many Glock switches still bear Glock’s logo,” the state admitted in its suit. “The popular association of the Glock brand with machine gun functionality runs so deep that many third-party auto sears are even sold with a copied Glock logo printed on them.”

Jennings and Glock did not immediately respond to requests for comment from the Daily Caller News Foundation. Four states, Connecticut, California, Maryland and New York, have passed bans on the Glock pistol, but a federal judge blocked Connecticut’s law on Second Amendment grounds.

Other states, including Maryland, Minnesota and New Jersey, have also sued Glock over the devices. Under current federal law, it is illegal to possess or manufacture a fully-automatic firearm that is not registered or authorized under the provisions of the National Firearms Act. A conviction for violating the law can lead to up to ten years in prison and a $250,000 fine.

Research by the Crime Prevention Research Center (CPRC) showed that murders with illegally-modified Glocks are less frequent than fatal lightning strikes, with only 40 people dying in attacks using the handguns since the start of 2021, while the National Weather Service confirmed 81 deaths from the meteorological event in the same timeframe.

Glock pistols are among the most popular in the United States, regularly appearing in lists of the most-sold firearms compiled by outlets like Guns and Guns and Ammo magazine. The company’s Glock 19X sold over 100,000 copies in less than six months after the pistol’s release, according to a 2018 press release by the company.

In addition to being popular among law-abiding citizens, Glock pistols are also used by numerous law enforcement agencies, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), which has issued versions of the handgun to its agents since 1997. Former Vice President Kamala Harris boasted on multiple occasions about owning a Glock pistol she acquired for personal protection.

news.title: Why Republicans are on the back foot ahead of US midterm elections
news.text:
Next week, tens of millions of Americans will head to the polls to elect their representatives to the 120th US Congress. The race for the US president attracts the lion’s share of global media attention every four years, but the midterms crucially shape the second half of presidential terms.

This year’s elections arrive amid a political pressure cooker of lawsuits, electoral disputes and accusations of interference by all sides of politics. 

After almost two years of a pliant Republican-controlled legislature, President Donald Trump is bracing for the first nationwide electoral test of his second term.

So, what are midterm elections, and how might the results on November 3 shape the United States until a new president takes the oath of office on January 20 2029?

What are the midterm elections?

Every two years, both chambers of Congress get a shakeup. All 435 members of the lower house, the House of Representatives, are up for election. Around a third of the 100 senators who sit in the upper house face voters, too. This cycle, 36 governorships will also be on the ballot, along with a smattering of state-level contests for legislators and local officials.

When they fall outside a presidential year, these elections are called “midterms,” marking the rough midpoint of a president’s four-year term.

As the US government’s chief legislative body, the make-up of Congress decides each party’s ability to pass federal legislation and scrutinise the president. Most presidents in modern American history have at some point navigated a divided Congress, where the opposition party controls one or both legislative chambers. 

What can we expect?

History tells us the president’s party is almost always punished in the midterms.

In the 2006 elections, during George W Bush’s presidency, Republicans lost 30 House seats. Four years later, the Democrats suffered a whopping 63 net-loss “shellacking” in Barack Obama’s first midterm test as president.

The Republican party is unlikely to defy this trend in 2026. Top election forecaster Charlie Cook has called a Democratic sweep of the House in November a “done deal”. Pundits project the Democrats will pick up at least five and as many as 30 House seats — enough to overcome the GOP’s razor-thin majority and take control of the chamber for the second half of Trump’s term.

However, the Republican majority in the powerful US Senate may be harder to overturn and could come down to the wire. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to win back the chamber, which will likely hinge on the results of about seven hotly contested toss-up races.

Why are Republicans on the back foot?

While these midterms follow a familiar script, they might also be set to break historic patterns.

In the Senate, polling suggests Democrats may be on track for some significant pickups, including in reliably “red” (Republican) states that voted for Trump by double-digit margins in 2024. 

The race in Kansas — currently a dead heat — could see the state elect its first Democratic senator in almost a century. Democrats appear to be competitive in Republican strongholds Ohio, Alaska and Iowa. Polls even suggest they could have a chance in Texas, where the party hasn’t won a single statewide office since 1994.

As the battleground map expands, Republicans are reportedly pouring millions of dollars into advertising to defend safe seats that could now be under threat.

So, why have these Republican strongholds — previously seen as unwinnable for Democrats — come into play this election cycle?

Of course, distinct, local dynamics are shaping individual races, such as the scandals plaguing Ken Paxton’s campaign in Texas and incumbent Senator Roger Marshall in Kansas. In Alaska, Republicans worry that a same-name challenger could confuse voters and siphon support away from Republican Senator Dan Sullivan in a tight race.

But the midterms are ultimately a referendum on the sitting president. And right now, Trump’s approval rating is under water in 47 of the 50 US states.

Americans don’t trust him on trade, immigration or the economy. Seven in ten think the country is headed in the wrong direction. One survey found 48% of Americans say they are financially worse off compared to when Trump returned to office in 2025.

Pollsters are also predicting that a sizeable enthusiasm gap could play into Democrats’ hands on election day. Nearly half of the voters for Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris in 2024 (48%) are very enthusiastic about voting in November. Less than a third of Trump supporters say the same.

Rusted-on Republicans might be unlikely to switch their political allegiance to the Democrats. But it could be just as damaging for the Republican Party if they don’t vote at all.

Is it a done deal?

While many commentators are predicting a “blue tsunami” will wipe out Republicans, others have argued there are reasons for caution when predicting the midterm result.

The Democrats remain deeply unpopular. Gerrymandering has tilted the electoral map in the Republicans’ favour. 

And in what are already the most expensive midterm elections in history, Republicans continue to hold a clear financial advantage. Elon Musk alone has donated more than a quarter of a billion dollars to Republican groups, including his own voter turnout operation.

Moreover, even though polling has been accurate in recent midterm cycles, it has famously missed before.

If Trump is so powerful, do the midterms even matter?

With Trump wielding a level of executive power unmatched in modern US political history, the midterms may seem a minor distraction with little enduring impact on his presidency. In May this year, he said “I don’t care about the midterms”.

Yet, if the Democrats can flip one or both chambers, they would gain the power to launch House investigations and block nominations for top judicial and government. Congress can also pass legislation that overrides or restricts funding for presidential orders. It could even set the stage for Trump to face an unprecedented third impeachment.

The results will also offer an early — albeit imperfect — indication of “where partisan winds are blowing” as both parties eye the presidential primaries that kick off in early 2028.

Regardless of whether the president says he cares about the midterms, on November 3, millions of Americans will show they do.
news.summary: Sitting presidents are almost always punished in the midterm elections – and 2026 is looking like it will be no exception.
news.author: Ava Kalinauskas,Senior Research Associate,United States Studies Centre,University of Sydney

news.title: Prominent Iowa Newspaper Endorses Josh Turek In Senate Race
news.text: The editorial board of prominent Iowa newspaper The Des Moines Register has backed Democratic Senate candidate Josh Turek over Republican opponent Ashley Hinson. It published its endorsement on Sunday, arguing that Turek would be “most likely” to remove “some of the external pressure on agriculture in Iowa,” namely through his pledge to “demand that President Donald Trump stop waging war on Iran and stop upsetting the markets for Iowa’s crop exports and inputs.” The economic fallout from Trump’s trade tariffs and rising domestic fuel prices tied to the ongoing conflict in Iran has hit farmers particularly hard, making it a crucial issue in races across America’s agricultural heartland. Democrats, trying to win back control of the U.S. Senate, hope to turn this frustration into votes for Turek and its other candidates. Although Iowa has voted Republican in Senate elections since 2008, the Cook Political Report lists Iowa's Senate race as a "toss-up." The Hawkeye State also has a history of voting for presidential candidates from both political parties. Trump won Iowa the last three election cycles, but before that, President Barack Obama won Iowa twice. Republicans are defending the governor's office, left open by GOP Senator Joni Ernst’s retirement, and three competitive Republican-held House districts. Turek responded to the endorsement in a post on Facebook, saying he was “grateful” for it. “We're going to win this race and deliver change for Iowa,” he added. Newsweek has contacted campaigns for Turek and Hinson for comment. Why The Des Moines Register Backed Turek Over Hinson The editorial board said Turek “is a compelling candidate in any environment,” but it stressed his commitment to improving things economically for Iowan farmers. Both Turek and Hinson have focused on the economic hardship facing Iowans throughout their campaigns, and both have called for an end to the war in Iran. Hinson has tried to distance herself from Trump, positioning herself as willing to work across party lines for Iowa and saying she was not scared to confront Trump over issues they disagreed on. Hinson called for an “immediate end” to the war in Iran last month, saying “Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn't have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran.” But this was a departure from her own voting record—she voted against bringing an immediate end to the war in Iran four times this year. The board touched on this when it said: “The current Republican-controlled Congress has made plain that only Democrats will push back on President Donald Trump’s damaging policies and his self-aggrandizing whims in any meaningful way.” It also praised Turek’s policy knowledge and ability to connect with people, citing his previous representation of Carter Lake and part of Council Bluffs in the Iowa House since 2023. The Des Moines Register’s Endorsement Record The Register, which has endorsed political candidates since at least 1912, has backed both Democrats and Republicans, but recent decades have seen it repeatedly swing toward Democrats. The Register did not endorse either Trump or former Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris in 2024 because its owner, the newspaper chain Gannett, said none of its outlets would endorse a presidential candidate, but they could still endorse local candidates. Gannett spokesperson Lark-Marie Antón told CNN at the time that the firm had made the decision because “we believe America’s future is decided locally – one race at a time.” Before that, The Register had backed Democratic presidential candidates Joe Biden in 2020, Hilary Clinton in 2016 and Barack Obama in 2008, according to a Noah Veltman compilation of newspaper presidential endorsements. While The Register broke its Democratic streak to support Republican presidential candidate Mitt Romney in 2012, it endorsed a Democrat in every other election between 1980 and 2004. Similarly, The Register has mostly endorsed Democrats in local elections - including all four U.S. House contests and Theresa Greenfield’s Senate bid in 2020, as well as Rob Sand for governor this year. Judge Dismisses Trump's Case Against The Register Last month, a judge dismissed Donald Trump’s lawsuit accusing The Des Moines Register and its former pollster of misrepresenting the state of the 2024 presidential race, rejecting the president’s claim that the newspaper’s poll coverage violated Iowa’s consumer fraud law. Trump filed the lawsuit against Selzer, The Des Moines Register and the newspaper’s parent company in December 2024, accusing them of fraudulently publishing inaccurate poll results to damage him and help Democrats, saying coverage of polls is not protected speech. The poll, conducted by Selzer’s company in the final days of October and released just days before Election Day 2024, showed then-Vice President Kamala Harris, the Democrats’ presidential nominee, capturing 47 percent of Iowa likely voters, to Trump’s 44 percent. Trump ultimately won the support of 56 percent of the nearly 2 million Iowans who voted. Trump, along with Republicans U.S. Representative Mariannette Miller-Meeks and former Iowa state Senator Brad Zaun, alleged the misleading coverage diminished their reputations, valuable time in the final days of the campaign, and campaign funds and resources. But Iowa District Judge Scott J. Beattie said that allowing the lawsuit and its “faulty” claims to proceed could have a chilling effect that “can discourage others from reporting on and debating public affairs.” He sided with pollster J. Ann Selzer and the newspaper in affirming that the poll and coverage of it were constitutionally protected political speech, not a commercial product. Trump’s legal team said after the ruling that the president plans to take his case to the Iowa Supreme Court. Early voting remains underway in Iowa, where voters have been able to cast ballots since October 14 and can continue doing so through November 2, one day before the state's November 3 Election Day. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: John Fitzpatrick and Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: The Des Moines Register's board argued Turek would challenge Trump over economic hardship facing Iowa farmers.

news.title: Neil Young sues Trump a 2nd time over unlicensed use of his music at rallies
news.text:
Canadian rock legend Neil Young is suing U.S. President Donald Trump‘s political fundraising committee for copyright infringement over the alleged misuse of ‌his song Rockin’ in the Free World at an October midterm elections rally.

The Toronto-born singer, who is a vocal critic of the U.S. president, alleged in a complaint filed in Virginia on Monday against the Trump 47 Committee that the song was played without ​a licence before Trump took the stage in Youngstown, Ohio, while supporting Republican midterm ⁠election candidates on October 12.

“On information and belief, the committee has caused the song to be played numerous times at other rallies designed to encourage Republican votes in the upcoming mid-term elections,” the court filing reads.

It goes on to describe the 1989 song as a “blistering anthem that contrasts the hollow promises of American political rhetoric with the harsh realities faced by the poor, homeless, and forgotten.”

“The song is the opposite of everything Donald Trump stands for,” the document continues, noting that its enduring popularity was recently recognized by Rolling Stone, which named it Vintage Rock Song of 2026 and that the anthem was recently performed live on stage by famous musical artists such as Bruce Springsteen, Dave Grohl and Dave Matthews.

It accuses Trump of being aware that a licence would be required to play the song at rallies and that Young had not or would not grant the licence.

This is the second time the musician has sued a Trump-associated body for using copyrighted material without permission. In 2020, he sued Trump’s re-election campaign for using Rockin’ in the Free World and Devil’s Sidewalk at campaign rallies without proper licensing.

That case was settled, according to the filing, with the campaign promising to never play the music again at one of its events.

The repeated use of Young’s songs at Trump rallies has damaged the singer’s reputation, the lawsuit argues, as a result of the implication that Young supports Trump’s political agenda.

Young is asking for $10 million in damages.

An outspoken critic of Trump, last year, the Canadian rocker released a song titled Big Crime, taking aim at the president.

Young first played the track criticizing the Trump administration at a show in Chicago with his band The Chrome Hearts in August 2025 and later posted the song’s lyrics on his Neil Young Archives website.

“There’s big crime in D.C. at the White House,” the 80-year-old rock icon sings in the chorus. Other lyrics aimed at Trump but not mentioning the president by name include “don’t need no fascist rules, don’t want no fascist schools, don’t want no soldiers walking on the streets.”

“Got to get the fascists out, got to clean the White House out, don’t want soldiers on our streets,” Young sings.

He also takes Trump’s signature slogan, “Make America Great Again,” and repeats throughout the song, “No more great again.”

Young, who is a Canadian-American dual citizen, has directly criticized Trump in the past. Last May, he told him to stop “worrying” about what Bruce Springsteen, another outspoken critic of the president, and other celebrities think of him.

Young’s comments came after Trump escalated his feud with Springsteen, calling for a “major investigation” into the rock legend after Springsteen branded the Trump administration as “corrupt, incompetent and treasonous” during a concert in England.

Springsteen and Young are not the only musicians to push back on appropriation of their music.

In June, Ariana Grande called out the Trump administration for attaching her music to its social media content. The Grammy-winning pop star wrote, “Please do not ever use my music ⁠in relation to this barbaric, inhumane, heinous nonsense,” after her 2024 hit Bye was played over a TikTok highlighting Trump’s immigration policy.

Responding ​to Grande, White House spokesperson Abigail Jackson said: “We’ll say this ​one last time: what’s actually barbaric, inhumane, and heinous are the criminal illegal ‌aliens ⁠who have injured and murdered innocent American citizens.”

Sabrina Carpenter and Taylor Swift have also condemned the use of their music by the Trump administration on social media. Carpenter’s song Juno was used in an official ICE video, a move she called “evil and disgusting.” Meanwhile, Swift had several of her songs removed from White House social media campaign videos.

Trump has repeatedly criticized ​Swift after she publicly endorsed Kamala Harris, having written in a past social media post, “I HATE TAYLOR SWIFT!” “Has anyone noticed that, since I said ‘I HATE TAYLOR SWIFT,’ she’s no longer “HOT?”

— with files from Global News’ Katie Scott and Reuters
news.summary: Young alleged in a complaint filed in Virginia that the song was played without ​a licence before Trump took to a campaign rally stage Youngstown, Ohio.
