Democrat strongholds came out in large numbers in the first few days, but so did Republicans in their strongest counties. As the days progressed, however, Democrats seem to have rolled off like they have in other states. Precincts in South Dallas are now seeing less turnout than in previous days, while counties like Montgomery, the burbs north of Houston, are chugging along. On X, it seemed to me that Collin County, another burb county north of the DFW metroplex, was going to be a bellwether. Between 85-90 percent of the county votes early and in person. Only 5 percent vote by mail, and under 10 percent vote on Election Day. So you can gauge how the county will go by looking at several days of early voting. 

Collin has gradually changed over the last decade. It was as deeply red a county as Texas featured in 2016, but in each successive cycle, it has voted less Republican than the rest of the state, with 2024's tally 2.4 percent more Democratic than the rest of the state. What does this mean? Let's assume the premise of a lot of polling — that James Talarico is ahead statewide by a couple points. If Collin County is slightly to the left of where the rest of the state is, you would expect Talarico to win in a county like this. He'd have to, in fact. Conversely, if Ken Paxton hangs on in a county gradually slipping away from Republicans, even if by a small margin, it's just not plausible to see how Talarico is going to build a margin big enough, especially when the youth vote is disappearing in the Lone Star State, too. 

Another three days of data, and Collin County is still leaning red by five points based on primary voting propensity. https://t.co/qapb3aN2fM— Duane Patterson (@Radioblogger) October 27, 2026

Could there be Republican crossover to vote for Talarico? Sure, it's possible. Likely? I wouldn't bet on it. And then there's the voters with no previous primary voter profile. These are either independents, or more likely, newer residents of Collin County. My timeline was full of proclamations assuring me every single one of the unaffiliated voters would be a Talarico voter, and that I should cope more. My instinct tells me a good chunk of people leaving blue states to red states like Texas with no state income tax are conservatives fleeing bad governance. I know a bunch of people from California that relocated to Texas, and California has only gotten bluer as a result. Why? Republicans are the ones leaving. So that's one metric to model what the margins might be — looking at the voter's primary ballot history. According to that, statewide, Theo Elections have the Democrats with a very narrow as of yesterday. Excluding those with no history or those who have voted in both primaries, if every primary-registered voter stayed true in the general, Democrats would have a bank of 3,200 votes out of 3.4 million cast thus far. Insurmountable, right? Using the same metric, primary propensity, on Election Day in both the 2022 and 2024 cycles, proven Republicans turned out twice as much as proven Democrats. That's 350-450,000 votes, depending on the turnout. Using that modeling, Paxton wins, even if every unaffiliated voter breaks for Talarico. For him to win, Republicans have to stay home on Election Day. The other modeling is even worse for the Democrats. Instead of looking at primary history, this method locates which precinct in which the early voter resides, and predicts how they voted based on how that precinct voted in the last two cycles. Using that methodology, also just as imperfect as primary participation weighting, but still instructive, this is what you come up with after a few weeks of data. 

stop dooming about Texas https://t.co/7guSe5vJNX— Ari Daniel Bradshaw (@AriBradshawAZ) October 27, 2026

Going by who's voting in which precincts and weighting for how those precincts performed in the last few elections, Democrats are not going to have a good day Tuesday next. 

Worst case for comparison. The first chart is a 2024 baseline: today’s 4.3M early voters, counted the way their precincts voted for Trump. This one scores them on 2024 Senate results (Cruz ran behind Trump) or Texas’s 2018 midterm swing, whichever is worse in each district. Statewide goes from R+11.1 to R+4.7, and TX-28 is the only seat that tips. Estimates, not a forecast. Reality is probably in between.— Ari Daniel Bradshaw (@AriBradshawAZ) October 27, 2026

Using Republicans' worst turnout in the last ten years as a baseline — Ted Cruz's Senate run in 2024 and Texas' 2018 midterm, you still come out to just under a five-point edge for Paxton. What will the actual numbers look like next Tuesday? An honest assessment is probably somewhere in-between these two models. Either way, they both point to a Paxton win unless three things all happen — Democrats reverse their slide in early voting the rest of this week, Republicans exhaust their early voters, and Republicans stay home next Tuesday. I'm not seeing anything thus far that indicate any or all of those happening. Looking east, or east of Texas, Georgia has limited early voting data available, but here's how it looks. The average of polling shows Jon Ossoff with a commanding 8.2 percent lead over Mike Collins. The white-Black split in early voting is roughly what polling uses in their makeup, but the age group split so far is different. Polling estimates the youth vote will be between 10 and 15 percent, and the seniors will be under 36 percent. After 13 days of early voting, the youth vote is under 9, and the seniors are over 40, but just barely. The polling is probably too generous to Ossoff, but Republican Election Day turnout has to be pretty dramatic for the upset to happen. In 2022, Herschel Walker won Election Day voting by over 10 points, but lost it in mail in and early voting. Collins will have to put up those kind of numbers or better to pull it off. Out west, the two most interesting states to watch in early voting do not have a Senate seat in play. But there are indicators of whether a blue wave is forming or not. In Nevada, Republicans had built a modest cushion with in person early voting, but Democrats wiped out that lead with mail-in ballots and built a modest lead of their own. Governor Lombardo is at the top of the ticket for reelection, and his path to victory four years ago was essentially heading into Tuesday tied in early voting, and then riding a wave of Election Day Republican turnout. If Democrats burn out their high propensity votes by mail, and Republicans chip away at in person early voting keeping the early vote close, it could result in a very similar victory for Lombardo. The more Democrats vote early, the redder Election Day voters are. In Maricopa County, Arizona, Republicans are having a nice run in early voting.

Put it all together, it's a mixed bag. There is definitely not a blue wave taking place. At least not yet. Any wave-type year would include a higher percentage of youth vote. It may happen on Election Day. If so, it'll be a long night. If they stay close to their previous norms or come in under that, the higher-than-usual turnout of seniors may have a lot of pollsters wiping egg off their faces Wednesday morning. The electorate thus far seems to be older, a little whiter, more enthusiastic than 2022, but not quite to 2024 levels of intensity. Kamala attempts to articulate the value of talking to children. news.title: 'The Only Way She Can Lose Is if They Cheat': Trump Warns of Fraud as Minnesota Senate Race Tightens
news.text: US President Donald Trump claimed on Monday, 26 October, that Republican Michele Tafoya could lose Minnesota's Senate election only if opponents cheated.His Truth Social warning came eight days before the 3 November midterms, as polling showed a competitive contest between Tafoya and Democratic Lieutenant Governor Peggy Flanagan. Trump provided no evidence of planned ballot manipulation.Tafoya, a former NFL broadcaster, is challenging Flanagan for the seat being vacated by Democratic Senator Tina Smith, who is not seeking re-election.Recent polling has suggested a competitive race in a state historically favourable to Democrats.Smith has accused Trump of laying the groundwork to undermine the result if Tafoya loses. Her criticism represents a political accusation, not evidence of an organised effort to overturn the election.Trump's Minnesota Senate Race Warning Targets Ballot CountingTrump wrote on Truth Social, 'The only way she can lose is if they cheat by playing games with the Ballots as they come in.'He urged supporters not to allow interference with votes after election day, without identifying who he believed might interfere. Trump added, 'The Federal Government will be watching closely.'The president did not identify any suspected wrongdoing or provide evidence of planned interference. His statement also did not establish that federal authorities had launched a specific operation to monitor Minnesota's ballot counting.Trump encouraged Minnesotans to support Tafoya and repeated his 'Complete and Total Endorsement' of the Republican candidate. He had previously endorsed her on 12 October, despite her efforts to distinguish herself from his political positions.Tafoya has presented herself as an independent Republican willing to challenge the president when necessary, despite receiving his endorsement. Flanagan's campaign has argued that electing Tafoya would give Trump a dependable ally in Washington.The latest warning places Trump's claims about election integrity at the centre of a Senate contest in which he is not a candidate.Minnesota Senate Race Revives Trump's Disputed Victory ClaimsTrump also used his post to challenge the official results of Minnesota's previous presidential elections, claiming he had been denied victories in the state.'I won Minnesota three times, but they didn't give me the Victories,' he wrote, before referring to Republican Richard Nixon's presidential victory there in 1972.However, official election records contradict Trump's assertion. Hillary Clinton defeated him in Minnesota in 2016, Joe Biden won the state in 2020, and Kamala Harris carried it in 2024.Minnesota has not supported a Republican presidential candidate since Nixon, making Trump's claim of three victories inconsistent with the state's certified results.Trump presented his disputed account of those elections alongside his warning about the upcoming Senate vote. However, the results of previous elections provide no evidence that ballots will be manipulated in November.In a statement posted on X, Smith accused Trump of laying the groundwork to steal the election if his preferred candidate fails to win. Her criticism reflected concern about the president's willingness to accept an unfavourable result, rather than proof of an existing scheme.Trump's post provided no evidence that either campaign was manipulating the election. Under Minnesota's absentee ballot procedures, accepted ballots may be inserted into counting machines starting 18 days before election day.However, no vote totals are produced until polling places close at 8pm on 3 November. The state's established procedures distinguish lawful early ballot processing from the unsupported allegations raised by Trump.Tight Minnesota Senate Race Challenges a Democratic StrongholdMinnesota has not elected a Republican to the US Senate since Norm Coleman won in 2002. That history initially made the open seat appear relatively secure for Democrats, although recent polling has suggested a closer contest.A Minnesota Star Tribune poll, conducted from 5 to 7 October among 800 likely voters, showed Flanagan leading Tafoya by four percentage points, 47 per cent to 43 per cent.The survey carried a margin of sampling error of plus or minus 3.5 percentage points. Its findings indicated a competitive race but did not establish who would ultimately win.On 20 October, the Cook Political Report changed Minnesota's Senate rating from 'Likely Democrat' to 'Lean Democrat', acknowledging improved Republican competitiveness without predicting a Tafoya victory.Tafoya has criticised the handling of fraud involving Minnesota's publicly funded programmes under Democratic Governor Tim Walz's administration. Flanagan, who serves as lieutenant governor, has faced political scrutiny over the administration's response.Those cases are separate from Trump's unsupported suggestion that ballots could be manipulated in the Senate election. They do not establish that Flanagan personally participated in criminal wrongdoing or that either campaign is involved in electoral fraud.Flanagan has challenged Tafoya over her relationship with Trump, while the Republican candidate has sought to appeal to voters beyond the president's political base.With the election scheduled for Tuesday, 3 November, both candidates face a competitive final week. Trump's warning adds another contentious issue to the race, although his allegations remain unsupported by evidence.

news.title: Schumer, Dems are quietly betting big on one sleeper race in the Deep South
news.text: National Democrats are getting aggressive in the homestretch of this election cycle, sending money and party figureheads to a state that, for decades, has been out of reach. Mississippi has been a Republican stronghold for the GOP in the Senate since the 1980s, but in a political environment that is proving tough for incumbents of the party in power, Democrats appear to smell blood in the water. But Republicans aren’t buying the last-minute play in the Deep South, arguing that it’s a reach, at best, to make the race competitive. DEMOCRATS SEE NEW CHANCES TO FLIP RED STATES — BUT A $400M GOP SPENDING ADVANTAGE COULD DERAIL THEIR PLANS "Largely, I think they’re just throwing s--- at the wall at this point," a GOP political operative told Fox News Digital. The Senate Majority PAC, a political action committee with close ties to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., reserved $1.2 million in advertising in the state to boost Scott Colom, a district attorney mounting a bid against Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. And major figures in the Democratic Party, like former Vice President Kamala Harris and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, have also made the trip or are set to appear in the state — Buttigieg is scheduled to hold a rally on Mississippi’s Gulf Coast on Tuesday. Jake Monssen, Hyde-Smith’s campaign manager, told Fox News Digital in a statement, "This is simply Washington insiders making a last-ditch effort to give life to Scott Colom's failing campaign." "Scott is bankrolled by the radical left because he is in lockstep with their agenda," Monssen said. "He supports tax increases, open borders, taxpayer benefits for illegal immigrants, and sex change surgeries for minors." Like in other races across the Senate map, Colom has a fight with history to contend with. Mississippi has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1982, and the Magnolia State has consistently supported President Donald Trump. TRUMP-BACKED SENATOR ADMITS GOP FACES NIGHTMARE SCENARIO IN STATE REPUBLICANS HAVEN'T LOST IN 90 YEARS But Colom believes that the ground operation he’s developed while national Democrats stayed away from the state is what would put him over the top against Hyde-Smith, not the last-minute support. "It could be enough," Colom told Fox News Digital. "I mean, the thing is, the people of Mississippi built this campaign." Colom went on the offensive against Hyde-Smith, arguing that she "refuses to debate, she doesn’t campaign." "Because of that, I was able to build momentum on the ground, which means now that it's getting attention, now that it's getting resources, I'm able to take advantage of it in a way that other candidates couldn't," he said. Republicans aren’t resting on their laurels in the state, however. The Senate Leadership Fund, a political action committee closely aligned with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., teed up a seven-figure ad buy there in response to Democrats’ spending. And Trump appeared in Corinth, Mississippi, on Monday to rally for Hyde-Smith. He made a similar pitch to voters that he’s done at every rally stop this midterm cycle: pretend he’s on the ballot. "In this election, if you would, I'm asking you to pretend that I'm on the ballot," Trump said. "And the reason is that when I'm on the ballot, exactly 49% more people show up." Jonathan Klingler, a professor of political science at the University of Mississippi, told Fox News Digital that the increased spending and national attention to a once-sleepy race have generated the "talking point of Mississippi as evidence for momentum and building a Democratic wave." THUNE MAKES BOLD PREDICTION ABOUT REPUBLICANS' SENATE CHANCES AS GOP PULLS MILLIONS FROM KEY RACES "So at least I'm not — I can't say whether that's the intent of the funding here or visits, but that is the effect," he said. There are also voter demographics that both Hyde-Smith and Colom have to contend with. Mississippi has the highest share of Black voters in the country at nearly 40% of the electorate. In order for Colom and "Democrats to be successful, they simply have to peel off a larger share of White voters," Klingler said. There’s another storyline underneath the headlines of this race, too. Hyde-Smith and Colom have a history dating back to the Biden administration, when the lawmaker blocked his nomination to serve as a district court judge in Mississippi. "Instead of saving himself the embarrassment of being denied a job twice by Hyde-Smith, Colom is running a campaign backed by Chuck Schumer, funded by George Soros, and built on pro-transgender and other far-left policies," National Republican Senatorial Committee spokeswoman Bernadette Breslin told Fox News Digital. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP That’s not Colom’s motivating factor, however. He had just left Trump's northeast Mississippi rally where he spoke to voters about their main concerns, "everybody I talked to, gas prices, grocery prices," and tariffs, he said. But Colom said his personal dispute with Hyde-Smith was not his primary motivation. "I'll tell you, as a Christian, I forgive her for that. That's not a motivating factor for me," Colom said. "I mean, as a district attorney, I have to prosecute cases where people lost their loved ones to gun violence. So, you know, and I’ve seen them forgive that person." "So that's not the motivating factor," he continued. "For me, it's really the betrayal of the America First movement, right? Like she was supposed to help President Trump get lower grocery prices. Well, she betrayed us. We're not getting lower grocery prices."
news.summary: National Democrats reserved $1.2 million in Mississippi ads for Scott Colom as they target Cindy Hyde-Smith's Senate seat in a GOP stronghold.

The assessment will be published on November 24 in Secrets, which chronicles his 55 years in journalism. Woodward, who still holds the title of associate editor at the publication, details his growing disillusionment with the tech billionaire after initially trusting him to safeguard the institution.

Woodward reveals that when he was preparing to publish a hard-hitting book about Trump, Bezos reassured him. “Don’t worry, I have your back, Bob,” he claims Bezos told him. “I’ll always have your back.”

However, Woodward now says that “always” turned out to be far shorter than promised. 

He writes that Bezos has been “compromising public trust in The Washington Post’s aggressive and independent journalism” out of deference to Trump. 

While noting that Bezos has not directly interfered in news stories, Woodward argues that the billionaire’s sweeping staff cuts, personal ingratiation with Trump, and overhaul of the editorial page have betrayed a proud legacy.

Woodward’s disillusionment solidified when Bezos decided to spike a planned presidential endorsement of Kamala Harris, declaring the paper would no longer endorse presidential candidates. 

“At the time, I thought, is he not reading his own newspaper or my books about Trump?” Woodward writes, adding that the timing made it look “like Bezos and the newspaper were capitulating to Trump.”

Bezos subsequently restricted the opinion pages to advocating only “personal liberties and free markets,” with no dissenting views. 

“I could only imagine the agony this kind of decision would have caused Kay or Ben,” Woodward writes, referring to legendary publisher Katharine Graham and executive editor Benjamin C. Bradlee.

Woodward also laments that Bezos has failed to publicly defend independent journalism against Trump’s intimidation tactics. “It pains me that Jeff Bezos has remained silent,” he writes. “It is not too late for media owners to prioritize moral courage over financial gain.”

In response, newsroom leadership defended the paper’s current direction. Executive editor Matt Murray praised the reporting and said Bezos had never interfered in news coverage, adding, “With Jeff’s backing, the company is getting back in shape and poised for our best decade.” 

Woodward also noted that Bezos has never tried to overstep the mark by meddling in editorial decisions. Indeed, The Post was the first to publish a look at Woodward’s memoir. 

Newly promoted CEO and publisher Jeff D’Onofrio added that Bezos “remains unwavering in defense of our work, our independence and the safety of our journalists.”

Veteran White House reporter Peter Baker, who worked for more than 20 years at the Washington Post before moving to the New York Times, reported on Woodward’s excerpts for the latter.

He has been a vocal critic of Bezos’s ownership of the storied title. In February this year, he railed against cuts to the Post’s newsroom, which eliminated around 800 journalists. 

“No struggling newspaper ever saved itself by becoming a worse and less essential product. But what’s happening today at the @washingtonpost is not just the latest devastating contraction of the news industry; it’s the gutting of an American institution vital for a healthy society,” the correspondent wrote on X.

That move was defended as a critical business decision, and as CNN’s Brian Stelter pointed out in Tuesday morning’s Reliable Sources newsletter, Bezos has poured cash into the Post since he bought the money-losing paper in 2013. 

“Perhaps Bezos would say he took a stand by bankrolling the Post’s financial losses year after year,” he said. 

However, as a disappointed Woodward notes, the billionaire’s bankrolling has cooled in recent years. “I believed at the time that Bezos would provide the finances for The Post to continue to operate courageously. Jeff delivered on his word, initially,” he said.

A Bezos rep has been contacted for comment.

Bob Woodward, the veteran Washington investigative reporter who helped uncover the Watergate scandal, has delivered a searing rebuke of Jeff Bezos in his upcoming memoir, which the New York Times has obtained ahead of its release. 

Woodward alleges that the Amazon founder turned his back on newsroom staff and compromised public trust to appease President Donald Trump.

news.title: Kamala Harris calls Trump administration 'most callous and corrupt' in American history
news.text: While on the campaign trail Monday for Democrats ahead of the midterms, former Vice President Kamala Harris offered some of her harshest criticism of the Trump White House yet, calling it the "most callous and corrupt and incompetent" presidential administration in American history. Twice during her speech at an event for David Crowley, the Democratic nominee for governor in Wisconsin, Harris accused the Trump administration of wielding an agenda of "brutality" against Americans. Though in her lambasting of President Donald Trump's character and leadership style, she didn't mention him by name once. "We in this room, I know, understand that the measure of the strength of the leader is based on who you lift up, not who you beat down," Harris said. "Unlike some other people who are constantly looking in the mirror, David is looking at the people. That's the kind of leader we want." KAMALA HARRIS CLAIMS GOP 'CHEATING' AHEAD OF MIDTERMS, SAYS SHE'S FOCUSED ON STOPPING THE 'MADNESS' Her more specific, policy-based attacks came against Rep. Tom Tiffany, R-Wis., Crowley's opponent in the gubernatorial race. Harris noted that Tiffany supported Trump's efforts to overturn the 2020 election based on unsubstantiated claims of widespread fraud, before framing the upcoming election as a test of longstanding democratic norms. "Let's talk about the fact that David's opponent denied the election of 2020. By the way, we won. Yes, you can call me former madam Vice President. We won that election," Harris said. She continued: "We are now in the phase of the moment in our democracy, while we can still hold on to it, where the people's voice reigns, where the will of the people reigns, where the power of the people is demonstrated by what we do to organize." MAPPED: THE STATES TRUMP AND TOP DEMOCRATS ARE TARGETING BEFORE ELECTION DAY At an earlier event on Monday, Crowley called Harris a "huge mentor" of his, adding that his wife loves her. Tiffany pounced on the connection in a social media post, accusing Crowley of sharing Harris' support for higher taxes, "taxpayer benefits for illegals" and "Green New Deal policies" that he argued would drive up energy costs. news.title: Jesse Watters Praises AOC's 'Upside,' And It Goes Way Downhill From There
news.text:
Jesse Watters on Monday described the “upside” of Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) in a potential run for president ― but his take on “The Five” quickly devolved into innuendo and a “white people” detour.

The Fox News host, playing provocateur, noted that Democrats Kamala Harris “cannot win,” Gavin Newsom “needs to be medicated,” and Pete Buttigieg is “boring and gay, which you never see.”

“AOC has the most upside,” Watters concluded.

“Upside?” co-host Greg Gutfeld interrupted. “Really? Jesse?”

“Downside, too?” Watters cracked.

They laughed, perhaps in a bro nod to Ocasio-Cortez accusing Watters of “sexualizing” her on his show earlier this year. (For his part, Gutfeld recently snarked about the congresswoman, “All I’m thinking about is her behind!”)

“She does have a lot of growth potential,” Watters said Monday in a brief effort to restore pseudo-seriousness. “Like when I saw her go to Michigan and she was eating different types of food. She was getting some fresh air and, like, being around white people. It was almost like she was seeing America for the first time. And that’s good.”

“Her problem is, people with money don’t wanna give it to her because she hates business,” he added, perhaps referring to her stance against corporate greed. “So she’s gonna have to pretend to like business in order to get money.”

Watters then described Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) as “too Jewish,” and Jewish co-host Jessica Tarlov made it clear she would not take his bait.

“I like that Jesse says that he would just like to see AOC with more white people, that that would make him more comfortable,” she said.

“It would make her more comfortable with us and America,” Watters replied.

“She feels fine about you,” Tarlov said.

“That’s not what she said,” Watters replied. “She accused me of sexual harassment.”

“I don’t wanna get between you two about that,” Tarlov said.

news.title: Trump fires back after Obama compares White House to Cheesecake Factory

Cindy Hyde-Smith, who is facing an unexpectedly competitive challenge from Democrat Scott Colom.“I’m here today in Mississippi for a very special reason: to stop a Marxist, radical-left, Soros district attorney from being elected to the United States Senate,” Trump told supporters.Colom has also received help from prominent Democrats. Former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigned in Mississippi last week, while Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock has encouraged Democrats to pay more attention to the state.Trump’s campaign blitz continues Tuesday with stops in Corpus Christi and the Lubbock area of Texas. Former NFL players, including former Texas A&M quarterback Johnny Manziel, are expected to join him.RELATED STORY | Democrats tout momentum as early voting rises ahead of midtermsThe president is also using the final stretch of the campaign to again raise concerns about voter fraud, despite scant evidence of widespread fraud.Trump posted on Truth Social on Monday that anyone reporting voter fraud in past elections or the 2026 midterms would receive $1 million “upon the arrest and conviction of those that created the fraud.”Trump also raised concerns about the Minnesota Senate race and urged supporters not to allow anyone to “play with the votes after the race is over,” adding that the federal government would be watching closely.With seven days until Election Day, candidates are battling over the economy, wars and control of Congress. But amid all the traditional campaign issues, the Cheesecake Factory has become an unexpected part of the closing argument.

news.title: New Hampshire journalist says he was blocked from covering Kamala Harris political event
news.text: A New Hampshire journalist said he was denied entry to an event Saturday featuring former Vice President Kamala Harris. "The reception that I've gotten at past Democrat events from activists, from staff has mostly been positive… which is what makes this situation so disappointing," New Hampshire Journal reporter Leonard Robinson told Fox News Digital in an interview Monday. Nothing compares to Harris's visit." Harris was on the campaign stump in the Granite State for Democratic New Hampshire Senate candidate Chris Pappas. DEM HANDLERS LASH OUT WHEN CAMERAMAN CONFRONTS THEIR BOSS ABOUT DEBATE: ‘NO PICTURES’ Robinson said he RSVP'd to an event hosted by Reproductive Freedom for All (RFA) by filling out a form sent to him by the Pappas campaign after being shut out of another Harris event hosted by the campaign itself due to spatial constraints, according to an email obtained by Fox News Digital. I think that's the real question that's gotta be answered here," Robinson said. New Hampshire Democratic Party Chair Raymond Buckley criticized New Hampshire Journal, calling the outlet "a partisan right wing site created to smear Democrats" and saying it "has rarely, if ever, received credentials to any Democratic or progressive event" in response to Robinson's X thread. NH Journal managing editor Michael Graham stood by Robinson, telling Fox News Digital, "This is a rare occasion for them to literally force Leonard out of, or one of us out of the event. And given Vice President Kamala Harris and her potential hopes to make history, it was really unfortunate that they would keep [out] a reporter from an award-winning member of the New Hampshire Press Association." It is unclear whether a miscommunication error among the Democratic organizers was behind the incident. Neither representatives for Harris nor the New Hampshire Democratic Party responded to Fox News Digital's requests for comment. A spokesperson for the Pappas campaign declined to comment. Harris has taken part in several campaigns for Democratic candidates ahead of the midterm elections. Her appearances also come as she weighs a potential 2028 presidential bid. news.title: Hegseth Faith Adviser’s Shocking Vile Posts Revealed
news.text:
A Pentagon official credited with shaping Pete Hegseth’s religious agenda has been exposed as a conspiracy theorist who regularly shares racist and homophobic posts online.

Ryan Higgins, a senior adviser to the defense secretary, is part of the team helping Hegseth bring Christianity more prominently into military life. 

But a damning CNN investigation published Tuesday has exposed that Higgins has an unsavory history that includes social media attacks on immigrants, gay couples and women.

Several sources told CNN that the adviser had helped shape the Pentagon chief’s religious messaging and played an important role in developing the new Office of Religious Affairs.

Higgins has rejected the idea of separation between church and state, while Hegseth has argued that military readiness requires spiritual strength.

His social media footprint is also riddled with bigotry.

When Trump circulated a video featuring the Obamas portrayed as apes in February, Higgins described it as “funny,” although he conceded it was in poor taste.

In March, Higgins warned about “the satanic cult of LGBTQ.” Two months later, he attacked adoption by same-sex couples, describing a male couple bringing up a child as “two dudes buying babies.”

Higgins has also denounced same-sex marriage and suggested transgender people need religious intervention.

He has also attacked immigrants and Muslims. In January, while discussing allegations of sexual violence involving migrants, Higgins wrote that immigrants were behaving like barbarians and sexually assaulting white women.

He has also claimed Islam promotes violence against nonbelievers and suggested Muslims might overthrow the British monarchy.

Women—and particularly female politicians—are another of Higgins’s regular targets.

He speculated, without evidence, about whether former Vice President Kamala Harris, 62, had undergone abortions, citing her age and making unsubstantiated allegations about her sex life. 

He also argued that women cannot feel fulfilled through professional success in the same way as through motherhood.

The adviser also expressed questionable views on the legitimacy of the U.S. political system.

Following Trump’s 2020 defeat, Higgins rejected Biden’s election victory and boasted on social media about buying an assault rifle. During the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol riot, he said electoral fraud—for which there was no evidence—meant the orderly transfer of presidential power was impossible.

These are apparently views he still holds. In June this year, ahead of next week’s midterms, he declared that he had no confidence in American elections and suggested the results were fabricated.

The Pentagon, however, is standing by its adviser. Chief spokesman Sean Parnell described Higgins as a valued member of Hegseth’s staff whose focus had been supporting troops’ spiritual welfare and developing the new office.

Two other sources speaking to CNN disputed the extent of his influence, describing him as one adviser in a larger team.

Parnell did not answer the outlet’s specific questions about the inflammatory statements, and Higgins did not respond to its requests for comment.

The Daily Beast has contacted the Pentagon for comment.

news.title: Cindy Hyde-Smith Says Just 9 Words After Being Called On Stage by Trump
news.text: President Donald Trump campaigned in Mississippi on Monday as part of a final stretch of midterm appearances that has taken him to several Republican-leaning states. The rally was held for Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, who faces a challenge from Democrat Scott Colom in a state that has long favored Republicans. The election could help determine control of Congress and state governments. "I’m here because Cindy’s doing great, but I just got to make sure. I can’t take a chance," Trump told the crowd, his voice audibly hoarse, as he urged support for Hyde-Smith. Colom was also at the rally site. Trump later attacked him from the stage, calling him a "Marxist radical" and a "fake" and "shameless phony who pretends to be a moderate." Before the president arrived, Colom said he had planned to listen to Trump’s supporters. "They actually deserve a senator that will listen to them, that actually cares about what they think, actually cares about what they’re going through," Colom said. Hyde-Smith Had Spoken Earlier at the Rally The brief exchange that circulated online was not Hyde-Smith’s only appearance at the event. She spoke earlier in the program, telling voters the Senate’s control was at stake on November 3 and asking them to send her back to Washington to be "that fighter with the president." Trump spoke for more than 80 minutes before inviting Hyde-Smith back onto the stage. She asked the crowd, "Is this not the best president in our lifetime?" and then promptly left. Trump responded, "That was a record," and, "That was great." The nine-word count refers to this later exchange, not to Hyde-Smith’s remarks across the entire rally. Newsweek has reached out to Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith’s office, her campaign and the White House for comment and is awaiting responses. Social Media Users Question the Brief Appearance Clips of the exchange circulated on X, including posts by Acyn and Aaron Rupar. Some social-media users described the moment as awkward and questioned why Hyde-Smith’s appearance was so brief. Others argued that the clip reflected the challenge Republican candidates can face when sharing a rally stage with Trump: his long speeches can leave them relatively little time to make their own pitch. Trump often invites candidates onto the stage during rallies and asks them to keep their remarks brief. Why Trump Is Campaigning for Hyde-Smith Mississippi is among the country’s most reliably Republican states, and Trump won it three times. Hyde-Smith remains favored, but Colom’s campaign has drawn national attention and Democratic spending. The Senate Majority PAC, which is aligned with Democrats, announced a $1.2 million television ad campaign supporting Colom. Former Vice President Kamala Harris also campaigned with him days before Trump’s visit. The contest is part of a wider campaign push by both parties ahead of the midterms. Voter discontent over inflation, the war in Iran and other aspects of Trump’s presidency has helped Democrats expand the number of House and Senate races they are contesting. Trump’s schedule includes further appearances in states he won in 2024, including Texas, South Carolina and Iowa, as well as a planned rally in Kansas. Hyde-Smith was appointed to the Senate in 2018 after Thad Cochran resigned and later won a special election to complete his term. She was the first woman to represent Mississippi in the Senate. Among 800 South Asian registered voters surveyed, 87 percent were Indian-Americans and the remaining 13 percent were Pakistani, Bangladeshi, Sri Lankan, Nepali, Bhutanese, Maldivian, Afghani, Khmer, and Burmese people.Among those who voted for Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election, 96 percent plan to cast their ballots in favour of a Democratic candidate in the upcoming polls.The survey found that 67 percent of South Asian Americans who voted for Trump still backed the Republicans, but 25 percent said they would support Democrats.Key Issues And Voter SentimentThe survey findings come as early voting has begun in several states, including Texas, where Democratic nominee James Talarico is in a tight race against Republican Ken Paxton, who is supported by Trump.Vasant Bhatt, a 21-year-old second-generation Indian American who had interned on Senator Ted Cruzs election campaign in 2024, said in a social media post that had voted for Talarico.I just cast my ballot for James Talarico. As a second-generation Indian American, I am thoroughly disgusted by the xenophobia, racial resentment, and increasingly brazen attacks on my identity, Bhatt wrote.The survey also highlighted concerns over discrimination, with 90 percent of registered voters saying they had experienced discrimination or knew someone who had, including 48 percent who said they had personally faced it.Discrimination Concerns And Voter EngagementIt comes as no surprise that a quarter of Trumps 2024 voters in our community plan to vote Democratic. This community can make the margin, and we are working to reach every voter who can, Chintan Patel, executive director of Indian American Impact, said in a statement.The survey also found that 16 per cent of respondents had not voted in any general election since 2020.Overall, 78 percent of those surveyed said their vote could bring about change, while 79 percent felt elected officials quickly lost touch with ordinary people.Another 67 percent said public officials did not care about the views of people like them, and 43 percent felt they had no say in government decisions.Impact In Battleground StatesThe survey highlighted the potential significance of South Asian American voters in closely contested states.Michigan is home to roughly 187,000 South Asian residents, and nearly 30,000 registered South Asian voters did not vote in 2022, more than the roughly 19,000 votes that decided the states 2024 Senate race.Texas is home to more than 700,000 South Asian residents, and nearly 100,000 registered South Asian voters did not vote in 2022.The Indian-American community has a strong presence in states such as California, Texas, New Jersey, New York, Washington, Illinois, Pennsylvania, and Georgia.In battleground states such as Georgia, Pennsylvania, Michigan, and North Carolina, even one or two per cent vote matters to swing an election in favour of a particular candidate.

news.title: Deep-red races tighten ahead of midterms
news.text:
With Democrats looking to accomplish a big wave election by winning Senate seats in longtime Republican strongholds like Texas, Florida and Kansas, even more surprising states have come into play as the November 3 midterm elections near.

Democrats have made moves into the Mississippi and South Carolina Senate races, states President Trump won by 23 and 18 percentage points in 2024, respectively. The Cook Political Report has recently moved both races toward the Democrats, with Mississippi going from "solid Republican" to "likely Republican" and South Carolina going from "likely Republican" to "lean Republican." 

In Mississippi, Trump held a rally for incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith following his 2024 opponent, former Vice President Kamala Harris, traveling there to back Democratic challenger, District Attorney Scott Colom. At the rally, Trump said, "I'm here because Cindy's doing great, but I just got to make sure. I can't take a chance."

Mississippi has not elected a Democratic senator since 1982. Colom is campaigning aggressively, including a viral ad about Hyde-Smith's previous comment about rising beef prices, in which she said people "have so many proteins to choose from." The ad has people saying "Pick another protein? ... I'd rather pick another senator instead."

In South Carolina, current Republican Sen. Darline Graham is looking to hold on to the seat she was appointed to after her brother Lindsey Graham died in July after serving in the Senate since 2003. However, polls show Democratic challenger Annie Andrews is within three points of Graham. Lindsey Graham beat Democrat Jaime Harrison by 10 points in 2020.

Trump recently campaigned in the state for Graham, while farmers in South Carolina recently told Andrews "it's going to be tough to survive" amid rising fuel and fertilizer costs. South Carolina Republican Rep. Ralph Norman said that while he will vote for Graham, "my family is not."

"Now, they’re grown and with their own children can do what they want," Norman added about his family's decision.

Two former South Carolina governors, Republican David Beasley and Democrat Jim Hodges, filmed an ad endorsing Andrews in the race, with Beasley saying, "one thing we do agree on right now is this country is too divided, and the political rhetoric has gotten way, way out of hand."

“That is why we're coming together today to support Annie Andrews."

In the House, Democrats are similarly looking to make gains in districts previously thought to be too deep red. On Monday, it was reported that they have invested more than $2 million into a number of those races, including one that President Trump won by 17 points two years ago that a poll has shown is now within the margin of error.

news.title: Everywhere You Find a Scummy GOP Ad, You Find a Republican in Trouble
news.text:
Vivek Ramaswamy’s closing message in his corrosive run for Ohio governor has been a monstrous smear campaign spearheaded by Amy Acton’s estranged mother, accusing the Democratic candidate of lying about her past where her mother stayed married to the man charged with raping Amy at the age of 12. Vivek is a special kind of cretin, but this is low even by his medical scam artist standards. 

The proliferation of these red meat ads relying on some kind of invented reality playing to people’s lizard brains is a big, big tell about where the Republican Party is entering the late stages of 2026. First, that JD Vance’s endorsement of it proved they are just like this now, and there is no bottom for a group of bottom of the barrel people actively embracing white supremacy and the cynicism of the seediest corners of the web. But we knew that already–that’s what 2025’s normie radicalization was about–now, there is a bigger tell to this bullshit.

These red meat ads are designed to appeal to people who are spending their kids’ college funds on Alex Jones supplements, and these ads are supposed to appear in GOP primaries, not two weeks out from the election. You’re supposed to have your base shored up by now as you tack to the middle late, and if you’re still out here herding MAGA cats, you’re probably not going to do very well, and all polling everywhere says they’re not. A 2024-style polling error would barely keep Blexas from happening. Looking across the entire constellation of various projections, a solid Democratic advantage in the House, and either a 51-49 or 52-48 Democratic Senate Majority, looks like the median outcome as of the final week of October.

These ads are a tell that Republicans aren’t confident that even their own voters will show up the way they need them to, and polls back that allegation up.

Many of these electeds who sold their agency to Trump are screwed, and they know it. They made Trump, at his least popular point, everyone’s dictator, and now just 1% of Republican ads even talk about the person they outsourced their entire central nervous system to. This is all heinous and destructive, yes, but it’s also extreme loser shit. No one who thinks they’re winning acts like this. This is the kind of stink that endures beyond one election cycle, and where little smelly squiggles follow you around forever like a soulless Pig-Pen. Vivek is never going to live this down, and for the rest of his life he will fear the company of others, wondering if they can smell him too. As long as they don’t have to watch Vivek swing a baseball bat, I suppose.

And Vivek isn’t the only one. There is extreme loser shit on display from the GOP as far as the eye can see. There are relentless attacks on the transgender community, outright appeals to every flavor of bigotry in the rainbow, and countless lies created out of AI slop costing the GOP well over a hundred million dollars. Everything that is happening in Republican campaigns right now has the energy of George Costanza, sweating bullets through his dress shirt as he realizes he’s not going to get his work in on time, and everyone can see through him in more ways than one. There’s a simple rule Vivek is creating for us, and it’s that where you will find red meat ads pointed at the gutter, you will find a Republican fighting for their political life, like Vivek who is down 3.7 points to Amy Acton, per the latest RealClearPolitics (RCP) polling average. Here’s just a sampling of a few more high profile races with this dynamic.

Ohio Senate

A GOP Senate Leadership Fund ad featuring detransitioner influencer Soren Aldaco accused Democratic candidate with good ads, Sherrod Brown, of pushing surgery on minors like her. One problem, she’s not from Ohio and had surgery in Austin in 2021 as an adult. If a Republican is cutting a relentless surge of campaign ads denigrating transgender people, it simply means they are in trouble because they have literally nothing affirmative to offer voters and have been backed into a political corner. They’re just hoping everyone in their state is as sad, small and bigoted as they are.

RCP Average: Dem +2.8

Michigan Senate

An AI ad picturing Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed (AES) playing a game with Hasan Piker holding cards reading “Death to America” is on the air thanks to GOP super PAC Front Line Action. Republican candidate Mike Rogers also said El-Sayed “believes America deserved 9/11,” an utterly slanderous and false claim. Trump has also recently taken to calling AES a “jihadist” at his rallies. The only consistent campaign message Republicans have demonstrated in this race is rank Islamophobia, which has been countered very well by AES’ message that his name is not why diesel costs over $6/gallon. I wonder who’s ahead in the polls!

RCP Average: Dem +2.6

Kansas Senate

Famed patient suer and cookie enthusiast Roger Marshall has found himself in a fight no one ever expected him to be in, but welcome to the consequences of impoverishing the farm economy. Marshall has so far been unable to reorient the race away from his years of haranguing poor pregnant women for money, and Blansas is a genuine possibility. Following the natural desperation that billows off him every time he speaks is an ad claiming his Democratic opponent Adam Hamilton “protected a pedophile,” using an unauthorized photo of children at a camp unconnected to the abuse, and the camp demanded that Marshall remove it. Another deceptive attack ad splices separate sentences from Hamilton, producing a quote he never said. The unhinged attacks on transgender people have also entered this race, furthering it along as a rule of what a Republican candidate in danger looks like.

RCP Average: GOP +0.3

New York Governor

The mayoral race was a hint at how the New York GOP had planned an entire campaign for governor around rank bigotry. They were all excited to oust Democratic Governor Kathy Hochul by tying her to that dreaded socialist with a funny name, Zohran Mamdani, but turns out he’s pretty popular and that’s a great plan to get her reelected! You can see the residue of this abandoned plan as they have pivoted to high-minded attacks on her, like this AI ad of a guy asking her, “Want some crack?”

October 3-5 Emerson Poll: Dem +12

Georgia Senate

Jon Ossoff is running a really good campaign, and his fervent message to punish all the law-breakers in the Trump cartel is clearly resonating in Georgia. At the start of this cycle, Republicans were licking their chops at the thought of flipping this state Trump won in 2024, now they’re emulating a classic Atlanta Falcons collapse while running deepfakes of Ossoff getting beauty treatments alongside a wave of attack ads against transgender people. No one has a dimmer view of the Republican electorate’s intellect than Republican politicians do, and this race is yet more proof of that fact.

RCP Average: Dem +8.6

Texas Senate

Running perhaps the least inspiring person in a cycle defined by well-below replacement-level GOP candidates, the Texas GOP has gone all in on bigotry as the only reason to be a Texas Republican. They have chased tons of people from the party, like many in the southern Latino firewall they won in 2024. A Black MAGA content creator recently got her first lesson in what Republicans want Republican spaces to look like after getting kicked out of a Paxton event. Take your pick of what proves their sweaty desperation in this race: from the deluge of anti-trans ads claiming that James Talarico wants to forcibly transition every kid in America, to the AI ads depicting Talarico in a dress, to one of him defacing a Bible with a crayon. It all tells the same story that Ken Paxton has no good reasons why you should vote for Ken Paxton, and he needs daddy Elon to unleash a ketamine-induced wave of resentment and bigotry to try to save the GOP from the looming catastrophe of Blexas.

RCP Average: Dem +2.2

“We’re still running transgender ads. It’s just not resonating. $100 million in ads, $125 million in ads, and nothing’s moved the needle here in Texas in a month in the Senate race,” former Texas GOP House Speaker Dade Phelan said to Texas Monthly. “Let’s be honest. The 8 to 10% of voters in the middle who are going to decide this election, when they hear stuff about boys in girls’ sports, they don’t even know what you’re talking about.”

That “he’s for you, Kamala is for they/them” 2024 commercial that lives rent-free in Beltway pundits’ heads wasn’t what won Trump the election. It was primarily inflation and an anti-incumbency bias. Anyone trying to throw transgender people under the bus in 2026 either simply wants to do that, or they still don’t understand anything about the 2024 election. There’s a reason why you can find so much of this bullshit in campaigns like that of Vivek Ramaswamy that are struggling; it gives you a window into why they’re struggling! They don’t understand why they won in 2024 either!

Nothing has substantively changed about the big macro dynamics that cost Kamala Harris the presidency other than who is in power, save for inflation and the anti-incumbency bias becoming even more acute. All these sweaty and desperate ads from Republicans are a tacit admission that they agree with Phelan that they are “freaking out” because their own voters are shaky, and that gives some insight into what a GOP operative told Axios last week about Mississippi of all places potentially being in play: “No Republican seat is safe this cycle.”

news.title: The Crime Issue Is Kryptonite for Democrats. It Doesn’t Have to Be.
news.text:
In June 2025, before Zohran Mamdani was elected mayor of New York City, he went on a popular internet show called Subway Takes. It’s what it sounds like: The show’s comedian host invites guests to join him on a subway car and then, as they rattle along, grills them about their hot takes on this and that subject. Mamdani was there to defend his take that he, a political newcomer, should run the city.

Ever charismatic, Mamdani cracked a joke at the host’s suggestion that he could simply lower the cost of matcha lattes to win over voters. Then they turned to a more serious subject: policing. The host pulled out a crumpled election mailer: “This says NYC can’t risk a mayor who supports defunding police,” he said.

Insha Rahman, who was watching at home, perked up, eager to see how Mamdani would respond. A public defender turned criminal justice expert and political strategist, she now leads the Vera Institute of Justice and its sister organization, Vera Action, a prominent national advocacy organization that, among other things, advises politicians on how to talk with the public about crime and safety. Since 2022, her team has counseled hundreds of Democratic candidates. Months before the Subway Takes episode, in fact, they’d talked with Mamdani to help prep him for moments like this.

Communicating about crime doesn’t come easy for Democrats, who in many ways are still haunted by the brutally effective “Willie Horton” advertisement that supporters of the elder George Bush deployed against his Democratic rival, Massachusetts Gov. Michael Dukakis, during the 1988 presidential race. Horton, who is Black, had been convicted for participating in a 1974 robbery and murder in Dukakis’ home state. After more than a decade in lockup, he was allowed to participate in a weekend furlough program. During one such furlough, he fled the state, broke into a white couple’s home in Maryland, and then knifed the man and raped the woman. Horton was re-incarcerated, in Maryland this time.

Dukakis hadn’t created the furlough program—a previous Republican governor had—but he’d supported it, and Bush harped on the case to take him down. Bush’s allies even trotted out the victims for a series of news conferences. Bush dismissed critics who said the ad was racist, but it clearly evoked age-old tropes about Black men posing a threat to white women. Bush won the election handily.

Republicans have spent boatloads on these sorts of ads ever since, scapegoating immigrants and people of color in an effort to depict themselves as the Law & Order party and Democrats as Criminal Coddlers—or, more recently, as the Defund the Police party. Last month, Trump referenced Horton while stumping for a Senate candidate in North Carolina, and Repubicans have dropped more than $100 million on crime ads during this midterm cycle, far outpacing Democrats, who spent about $35 million, according to an AdImpact analysis of federal races in late September.

“The tough-on-crime narrative is a really powerful tool that reactionaries trot out every two to four years so that they can win elections, and the consequence of that has been disastrous in communities like mine,” Rep. Summer Lee (D-Pa.), who leads the Congressional Community Safety Caucus, lamented during a recent roundtable discussion. “It’s almost like watching the Titanic over and over and over again…We can never just avoid the iceberg.”

Time and again, Lee told me in an interview, Democratic candidates have struggled with communicating about crime and justice issues. Some try to play the Republican game, insisting they’ll be equally tough on crime—or tougher!—and accuse rivals of supporting the January 6 rioters and child predator Jeffrey Epstein. Others duck and pivot to more favorable topics, hoping to avoid the issue of crime altogether. But Rahman’s team at Vera, which has done extensive polling, and has the ear of many Democratic lawmakers, including Lee, is convinced that neither strategy is effective.

Instead, she and her colleagues advise Democrats to lean into conversations about crime—to go on the offense and establish their own positions straight out the gate, without mimicking their opponents. “What we’ve seen from our multiple rounds of polling and message testing and studying this issue and working on races,” Rahman said during a talk at the Democratic National Convention’s summer convening last year, “is that voters are really clear what Republicans are about when it comes to this issue…And when we ask, ‘What do you think Democrats stand for,’ they say, ‘I don’t know, I don’t know. What’s their brand? Do they care about this issue?”

“And the answer is, Democrats do,” she said enthusiastically.

In advance of the midterms, Rahman has been pushing candidates to seize the moment as Trump’s version of toughness—masked ICE officers wreaking havoc in American cities—has grown increasingly unpopular. This is the time, she says, for Democrats to build their brand by explaining, in detail, how they’ll improve public safety by means of everything from better policing to violence intervention programs to investment in schooling and affordable housing. The winning strategy, she believes, is to flip the Republican frame and focus not on crime and fear, but safety and solutions. (“Serious About Safety” is her preferred slogan.)

Dems need to “put Willie Horton to bed once and for all,” she says. And with crime at historically low rates, she believes they can—if only they are willing to get a little louder.

Rahman, 45, immigrated to the United States in 1994, a year Democrats were deeply invested in out-toughing Republicans on crime. That September, President Bill Clinton signed his controversial crime bill, which allocated billions of dollars to policing and prisons, enacted stricter criminal penalties, and arguably fueled mass incarceration more than any other legislation in modern US history.

Rahman was only 14 then, with other matters on her mind. She had just moved to an all-girls boarding school in upstate New York, a major change in pace after her childhood in Saudi Arabia, where her dad worked as as surgeon at a hospital run by an oil company. They’d lived on a diverse American compound with neighbors from all over the world. “My family is ethnically Indian,” she explained in a recent interview. “Suddenly I was in upstate New York, where my foreignness felt very pronounced. That’s what I was thinking about in 1994.”

It wasn’t until she attended college at Vassar, also in New York, that she began thinking more about the justice system. Her freshman year, she joined a program that brought students into Green Haven maximum-security prison to take classes with incarcerated men; the experience opened her eyes to the harshness of the criminal justice system. After law school, she became a public defender in the Bronx for five years before joining the Vera Institute, where she hoped to change some of the harmful policies she’d witnessed on the ground. Her early work included lobbying for a bail reform law in New York and serving on a commission to close the notorious Rikers Island jail. She helped sue the Trump administration last year, after it cut $5 million in Vera’s funding. This year, she was named the institute’s president and director—the first woman, Muslim, and immigrant to hold the position since the organization was founded 65 years ago.

The project to get Democrats talking smarter on crime kicked off in 2022, when Rahman was working with Vera Action and feeling frustrated by the backlash to progressive criminal justice reforms. During the pandemic lockdowns of 2020, the murder of George Floyd by a police officer in Minneapolis had sparked nationwide protests and a rallying cry to “defund the police.” These demands never materialized—police departments kept their massive budgets—but something else happened: Homicides spiked across the nation. By 2022, with midterms approaching, Democratic candidates were panicking and rolling back police accountability laws. “Fights about ‘defund’ dominated the conversation, as opposed to meaningful debate about safety and justice,” Rahman recalls. 

She wanted to better understand how voters were feeling, and whether the shift back toward tough rhetoric was necessary, so her team started commissioning polls. They knew that people were worried about crime—the New York Times interviewed one voter who was saving for a bulletproof vest to protect himself from lawlessness. But when asked to choose between a tough-on-crime approach (more resources for police, harsher bail laws, longer prison sentences) and a “serious about safety” one (getting illegal guns off the street and investing in preventative measures such as schooling, housing, jobs, and mental health and addiction treatment), 53 percent of respondents preferred the latter. That number grew to 56 percent in 2023, dipped as Trump ran for a second term, and then rebounded to 59 percent by early 2026. The results held across parties, and in swing states like North Carolina and Wisconsin. “It’s a broad consensus,” she says.

The polling showed something else, too: Traditional ads of candidates flanked by police weren’t performing as well as they once did. In Virginia, a majority of respondents favored a mock “serious about safety” ad over tougher ones by both Republican and Democratic candidates—Black, Latino, and Gen Z voters across political parties were especially likely to prefer it.

Many Democratic candidates have picked up on this, Rahman says. Take Baltimore Mayor Brandon Scott, a Democrat who, while running for reelection in 2024, ran ads crediting his city’s 20 percent decline in homicides in part to afterschool programs, not just better cooperation between the police and the community.

During his successful 2022 US Senate campaign, Pennsylvania’s John Fetterman ran an ad in which a burly, no-nonsense sheriff defended Fetterman’s record of pardoning nonviolent criminals when he was lieutenant governor. “He took that standard tough-on-crime ad and turned it on its head, using law enforcement to tell a different story about what makes communities safe,” Rahman told me.

Since 2022, her team has coached more than 200 candidates—including about 60 this midterm cycle—on the “serious about safety” approach. Among them were Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass and her challenger, Nithya Raman; Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan; and Wisconsin gubernatorial contender David Crowley. The team also has briefed the Democratic Attorneys General Association, the Democratic Mayors Association, and even a Republican candidate in Kentucky, showing them polling results and ads that have worked well, helping candidates prep for debates, and offering advice on policy platforms.

The Vera crew tailors its emphasis by region: Wisconsin voters, their polling shows, are particularly concerned about the overdose crisis, whereas Democratic politicians in California and New York need to spend more time confronting Republicans’ “disorder” narrative, which accuses Democratic leadership of allowing urban violence to go unchecked.

While some candidates find Rahman’s advice intuitive, others require convincing. “It’s a shock to the system. There’s a fear that a Democrat really weighing in on the public safety debate is just gonna get trounced,” says Benjamin Heller, a program manager at Vera. 

As a former law enforcement staffer in the UK, Heller recommends that candidates highlight the police as an important part of the puzzle, acknowledging that officers are overworked and could use help addressing mental health or addiction crises so that they can focus on solving violent crimes. “Police feel really seen when they’re told, ‘You guys aren’t social workers. We see you guys are responding to everything and we expect you to somehow do everything,” he says.

Mamdani, whom Heller briefed, used a similar message in his 2025 Subway Takes video. “No matter how many pieces of literature you get sent, I’m not defunding the police,” he said after the host brought up the accusatory mailer. “I’m actually working with the police to create public safety, by ensuring they can do their jobs, focused on serious crimes, and creating a Department of Community Safety that will focus on mental health, homelessness.”

“So technically the police force will stay the same, but there will be more people doing other stuff,” the host replied, kicking off to a humorous exchange.

“It just came together really beautifully,” Rahman says. Mamdani’s response had been, almost verbatim, what her team advises—and polling shows it’s popular with voters.

Not every campaign is so successful. In 2024, Vera staffers met with Vice President Kamala Harris’ then-campaign manager, Julie Chávez Rodrguez, and were pleased to see how her first ad, set to Beyoncé’s “Freedom,” contrasted Trump’s approach with her own: Trump wants a country “of chaos, of fear, of hate,” she said in the ad. Harris then highlighted her vision for affordable health care, reproductive rights, and crucially, safety from gun violence. “The fact that a Democratic candidate actually put safety front and center in a 30-second ad about who she is—I could see our fingerprints all over it,” Rahman told me.

But Harris’ campaign’s strategy soon pivoted to tougher ads touting Harris’ background as a prosecutor. At the DNC that year, Rahman warned that framing the race as “prosecutor vs. felon,” as the campaign was attempting, wouldn’t work—it hewed too close to Republican tough talk. “If Kamala Harris says, ‘I’m for the people, and here’s what I stand for, which is safety and justice,’ and contrasts that with, ‘Donald Trump is only out for himself,’ that is actually the most winning statement,” Rahman said at the time.

Rahman took an important lesson from Harris’ defeat. “If voters are hearing Republicans talk about being tough on crime, they’re like, ‘Yeah, that’s just who they are.’ When they hear that from Democrats, they think that’s not sincere,” she told me. “It just undermines their credibility and bolsters the GOP’s tough-on-crime argument.”

In a national poll this year, Rahman’s team asked people which party was more trustworthy on crime, and found that Democrats’ score actually declined by 10 percentage points when they tried to invoke their own tough rhetoric. “You can’t battle them on their narrative turf. You’ve got to get off their playing field and onto your own.” 

Last summer, with Trump moving fast and breaking things in Washington, Rahman returned to the DNC to make her pitch on the main stage. Chair Ken Martin introduced her personally. “The research that they’re doing is really seminal,” he said, and gives “people the right way to frame the conversation.”

Rahman urged the Democratic candidates in the crowd to “go on the offense” and call out Trump’s ICE and National Guard deployments as a political power grab. “This tough-on-crime rhetoric and actions, which historically I think Democrats have seen as a win for Republicans—it is actually a liability right now,” she said, and Trump’s cuts to Medicaid, food assistance, and services for crime victims were not making communities safer. With the homicide rate at a 75-year low, soft-on-crime attacks weren’t landing like they used to. Trump, Rahman warned her crowd, would take credit for the low crime rates, even though, as The Atlantic recently pointed out, murders were already on the decline when he took over, and 6 of the 11 states where the rates are falling the fastest are “sanctuary” jurisdictions whose Democratic leaders won’t cooperate with ICE.

“Crime is coming down, but don’t let Trump take credit,” Rahman told them. Say, “It’s going down in spite of him, and because of Democratic leadership—like mine.”

The DNC speech didn’t go over as well as she’d hoped: Right-wing media took a comment she’d made about migrant crime out of context, and even some moderate Dems weren’t impressed. “‘Serious about Safety’ feels more like a college sex talk topic during freshman orientation than a serious message for Democratic candidates,” John Anzalone, a leading Democratic pollster, tweeted afterward. “This is not good advice. It is DC-think in a bubble.”

The slogan “is catchy,” Sarah Pierce, director of social policy at Third Way, a think tank supporting center-left ideas, told me recently, “but it fails to state what voters are actually worried about, which is crime.” Gallup polling in March found that even if the low homicide rates make people feel more secure, 68 percent of respondents still said they worry “a great deal” or “a fair amount” about crime.

But others at the DNC were persuaded, including some members of Congress. The Congressional Black Caucus has partnered with Rahman’s team on a “Serious About Safety Majority” campaign to help Democratic candidates talk about public safety on the campaign trail and, if they take back Congress, to introduce relevant legislation. “They’re really trying to figure out ways of steering the Democratic caucus in a different direction,” notes Rep. Lee, who is running for reelection in Pennsylvania. 

They’re teaching lawmakers “how we can push back against the Trumpian narrative and go on the offense,” says Rep. Shontel Brown (D-Ohio), another member of the caucus, who appreciates the valuable data the Vera team has provided. 

“A lot of politicians need to see the proof in the pudding—to see they can survive these election cycles, that there is a pathway for them to be brave and honest without losing their jobs,” Lee adds.

Rahman’s efforts seem be shifting the Overton window on Democrats talking about crime. In 2022, she could count on one hand the number of candidates taking her advice. Today, almost “every single Democratic nominee for US Senate—in Michigan, in Florida, in Maine, in Texas—is running a Serious About Safety approach,” she told me. One outlier is former Gov. Roy Cooper of North Carolina, who has leaned on the old Bill Clinton-style rhetoric and maintained a solid lead in his bid for a US Senate seat. (Trump has suggested that Cooper’s prison release policies are akin to those of Michael Dukakis; old habits die hard.)

Whether the Democrats can make themselves heard over Trump’s fearmongering is an open question, but Rahman says she’ll keep encouraging them to try. In a recent poll, when Vera Action asked voters which party is more responsible for declining crime, they gave Republicans a 10-point advantage. But that lead disappeared completely when respondents learned that the decline began before Trump took office and after Democrat-led cities implemented strategies to prevent violence. “The problem may be that many voters are simply not hearing from Democrats,” the Vera team concluded.

The Dems, in other words, are leaving money on the table. Rahman wants them to grab it.

news.title: US midterms: How Jagjit Singh lobbied hard for Indians to become US citizens
news.text:
The US midterms are right around the corner – just eight days to be exact. Amid the hype and hullabaloo around the polls, there’s a lot of chatter about the growing importance of the Indian-American community and its participation in the US electoral process – be it as a lawmaker or a voter.
As of today, the United States has approximately 2.6 million eligible Indian-American voters, according to the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. Moreover, there are six Indian-Americans known as the ‘Samosa Caucus’ in the US Congress.
But the Indian factor in the US polls wouldn’t even be possible if US President Harry Truman hadn’t signed the Luce-Celler Act in 1946, which made people of Indian descent eligible for naturalisation as US citizens. And interestingly, the Luce-Celler Act was the result of a struggle by a Punjabi businessman who went by the name of Jagjit Singh, also known as JJ to his friends.
As we gear up for the much-anticipated midterm elections, let’s remember the man who made it all possible.
The early life of JJ Singh
JJ was born on October 5, 1897, in Rawalpindi in what is now the Punjab province of Pakistan. As a child, he often accompanied his father, who was a judicial officer, to different parts of the Punjab province.
As a young man, around 1920, Singh joined the agitation in Punjab following the Jallianwala Bagh massacre. According to a Khalsa Chronicle report, following Mahatma Gandhi’s release from prison in 1924, he expressed dissatisfaction with Singh over his use of violence, particularly in the Lahore unrest of 1919.
Unhappy and disillusioned, JJ Singh left India to study law in the United Kingdom. However, his interest moved to apparel wear. He soon got into the business of importing silk fabrics, handlooms, and other such items from India, and selling them abroad with assistance from his cousin.
JJ Singh arrives in the US
In 1926, his apparel work brought him to American shores, specifically to present his wares at the Sesquicentennial Exhibition in Philadelphia. He then went on to open a store in Philadelphia and another fabric store on New York’s 5th Avenue.
Soon, his business was booming, and he became known in influential circles. In the mid-1930s, he set up the Indian Chamber of Commerce in the US as an attempt to facilitate better trade relations between his country of business and British India.
He also joined the India League of America (ILA), a non-profit organisation which champions the interests of the Indian-American community in the US.
JJ’s fight for Indians to be granted citizenship rights in US
In December 1941, JJ took over and was elected president of the India League. He quickly threw open membership to the ILA to include not just Indians but an array of Americans in public life, such as writers, civil rights campaigners and peace activists.
He also set up another League office in Washington DC, which allowed him to grab the attention of lawmakers at Capitol Hill.
As the head of ILA, he spoke on issues like the Bengal famine, horrors of British colonial rule in India, and Japanese military advancement in South Asia.
 A newspaper clipping from Aug 9, 1943 titled "A Voice for the 400 Million, features Sardar JJ Singh, president of India League of America. Image Courtesy: @SAADAonline/X
It was under his leadership that the ILA also began advocating for the rights of Indians in the US, namely citizenship rights. In 1923, the US Supreme Court’s ruling in United States vs Bhagat Singh Thind had effectively refused naturalised citizenship to Indians.
Taking on this cause, JJ realised that it would require convincing the House and the Senate to rewrite immigration law to get around the Supreme Court. He roped in US Representative Emmanuel Celler, a Democrat with a pro-immigration stance, and the wife of TIME magnate Henry Luce, Claire Booth Luce, who was elected to the US House of Representatives as a Republican from Connecticut, to help him find a way to get Indians citizenship.
The duo then penned the Luce-Celler Act and introduced it in the House in 1944. Meanwhile, JJ Singh continued to lobby for the bill by meeting senators and engaging in a sustained campaign.
Finally, in 1946, the bill passed in Congress, and it was signed into law by President Harry S Truman on July 2, 1946. According to The Better India, after the ceremony, Truman handed over the pen he used to sign the Luce-Celler Act into law to JJ Singh.
Through this law, Indians could finally become Indian citizens. It also allowed a quota of 100 Indians to immigrate to the United States per annum. Years later, the Immigration and Naturalisation Act of 1965 did away with the quota system altogether. Instead, it established a policy that sought to reunite immigrant families and enabled more skilled labour to move to the US in search of a better life and opportunities.
JJ’s legacy lives on
JJ returned to India in 1959 and settled in Delhi until his demise in 1976. Interestingly, his sons, Man Mohan and Manjit, migrated to the US.
His legacy continues with Sabrina Singh, his granddaughter. In 2016, she served as the regional communications director for Hillary Clinton’s presidential campaign. And in 2020, she served as Vice President Kamala Harris’s press secretary.
 JJ Singh's granddaughter, Sabrina Singh, served as US Vice President Kamala Harris's press secretary. File image/AFP
Just imagine, had it not been for JJ Singh and his tireless efforts, Indians probably wouldn’t have been able to become US citizens and play such a crucial role in US politics. Of the approximately 5.2 million people of Indian origin in the US, 2.6 million are eligible voters. And while they are a small factor in the overall picture, their numbers are concentrated in places where margins are thin: Pennsylvania, Michigan, Georgia, Texas, New Jersey, and the suburbs around Atlanta and Washington.
