news.title: Trump has some support for an illegal 2028 bid for reelection, poll finds
news.text:
Despite President Donald Trump’s plunging approval ratings it would appear some Americans still back him for an unconstitutional third term in office. 

While Trump himself has blown hot and cold on the idea, a new poll indicates there are voters who want the 80- year-old commander-in-chief to run again in 2028. 

Eight percent of those surveyed in a New York Times/Siena poll still support Trump’s reelection. Although clearly a minority view, Trump still managed to receive more support than some of his allies. 

Trump has suggested he could run for a third term as recently as last week, claiming once again that he was “cheated” in the 2020 election.

“I don’t know who is going to be your next president, and I think the law said - I’m not 100% sure - but I think the law says I’m not allowed to run again,” he said at an Iowa rally.

​“Well, the one thing is different: they cheated us on the second one because we won it three times,” Trump said. ‘So I think I have the right to run again.”

​The New York Times/Siena poll, which was carried out using 3,494 voters from October 12 until October 19, looked at a number of high profile potential GOP nominees.

​Vice President JD Vance was the frontrunner, with 33 percent of respondents planning to vote in a Republican primary saying that they would nominate him for president.

​When asked previously whether he would endorse Vance, Trump dismissed speculation about the vice president launching his own bid for the presidency.

​“He's a very talented person and a very good person, but literally, I don't think we've ever talked about it,” Trump said earlier in October. “It's early, very early.”

​Secretary of State Marco Rubio came in second in the poll, with 23 percent of those surveyed backing him. 

Outgoing Florida Governor Ron DeSantis was backed by just three percent of respondents, much lower than Trump’s eight percent, while just one percent of voters said they would vote for Donald Trump Jr.

​Less than one percent of those surveyed said that they would vote for journalist and podcaster Tucker Carlson; Trump’s rival in the 2024 Republican primary, Nikki Haley; or Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

​The poll also examined the other side of the political aisle, asking respondents planning to vote in the Democratic 2028 primary who they would nominate for president.

Former Vice President Kamala Harris received the most support from those surveyed, topping the poll at 12 percent.

​Harris was closely followed by fellow Californian Gavin Newsom, the outgoing state governor, who received 9 percent of respondents’ support. 

Seven percent backed former Transport Secretary Pete Buttigieg, while Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez was supported by 6 percent of those surveyed.

​Four percent of voters backed Senator Jon Ossoff, who has made headlines in recent weeks for his remarks about Trump’s close aide, Natalie Harp.
news.summary: President Trump has suggested could run once again because he was ‘cheated’ in the 2020 election

news.title: Can Democrats Win Back Labor?
news.text:
The Lordstown plant is in the Mahoning Valley, once the second-largest steel-producing area in the country. Since the nineteen-seventies, the valley, home to Youngstown (“Steeltown, U.S.A.”), has lost more than fifty thousand well-paying steelworker jobs. At its peak, the Lordstown plant employed more than fourteen thousand people; at the time of its closing, it was the last large blue-collar anchor left in the area. Amid the industrial Midwest’s acute economic decline, this part of Ohio has become a bellwether for disaffection among working-class voters.
For decades, the Mahoning Valley, which is primarily made up of Trumbull and Mahoning counties, was one of the country’s most reliably Democratic regions, and a major part of Brown’s base. But in 2016 Donald Trump narrowly flipped the area, and, eight years later, support for him in Ohio had grown so much that Brown, a staunch labor Democrat, was unable to sufficiently distance himself from the top of the ticket, despite outperforming Kamala Harris by nearly eight points. Brown lost the valley, and the race, to Bernie Moreno, a luxury-car dealer from suburban Cleveland, in the most expensive non-Presidential election in American history, according to AdImpact. Many observers credited the crypto lobby, which spent forty million dollars to defeat Brown, who, as the chair of the Senate Banking Committee, had pushed for more regulation of the industry. But, ultimately, Brown lost because many working-class voters had moved on from the Democrats. “Soon as I saw the Mahoning Valley went down, I thought it was done,” Green recalls Brown telling him over the phone. “I got to win the Mahoning Valley.”
Two years later, Brown is hoping to return to the Senate by defeating Jon Husted, the Republican lieutenant governor who was appointed to the state’s other Senate seat after J. D. Vance became Vice-President. (The election is only to complete the final two years of Vance’s term.) The race is crucial to Democratic hopes of winning back the Senate, and is already on track to match or surpass the 2024 spending record. Brown has sharpened his populist messaging to focus on the rising cost of living and the growing backlash against data centers, and his success may reveal whether his party is able to reclaim the working-class Rust Belt voters it has been hemorrhaging for decades.
Earlier this month, I drove past the Lordstown plant, which contains more than six million square feet of manufacturing space and now stands barely used, a sort of physical embodiment of the vicissitudes of deindustrialization. Its travails over the past decade have been a major political liability for Trump, and function as a microcosm of the struggle to create industrial jobs in an economy that has devalued them for the past half century.
In 2017, at a packed rally in nearby Youngstown, President Trump implored his audience, “Don’t move. Don’t sell your house.” The valley’s factories, he promised, would be “all coming back.” By then, G.M. had already cut one of its three shifts at the Lordstown plant. To divert outrage after it shut down entirely, two years later, Trump appeared to blame Green, the union leader, personally for the plant’s closure, writing on Twitter that Green “ought to get his act together and produce.” (One of the actual culprits was Trump weakening the Obama Administration’s fuel-efficiency standards, which reduced the need for companies to build small cars like the Cruze.)
Later, trying to save face, Trump pushed G.M. to sell the plant. An electric-truck startup called Lordstown Motors bought it. Weeks before the 2020 election, Trump showcased one of the company’s trucks on the White House lawn. “Beyond the plant,” he said, “it’s incredible what’s happened to the area. It’s booming now.” But the following year one of the Lordstown Motors’ prototypes burst into flames on its first-ever road test. Soon afterward, an investment-research firm alleged that the company had made misleading claims about pre-orders. (An S.E.C. probe later found the company had misled investors; Lordstown Motors paid nearly twenty-six million dollars to settle the S.E.C.’s charges, though it did not admit to any wrongdoing.) In 2023, Lordstown Motors filed for bankruptcy.
By then, the plant had been purchased by Foxconn, a Taiwanese electronics manufacturer, which did little with the property until last year, when it sold the site to SoftBank, a Japanese investment firm. The plant is now part of the Stargate project, a seven-site, five-hundred-billion-dollar A.I.-infrastructure build-out backed by Trump and involving Oracle, OpenAI, and SoftBank. Stargate’s future has looked increasingly uncertain after Oracle, already heavily leveraged, filed paperwork to shield itself from upcoming debt payments for another Stargate data-center campus, in New Mexico. Still, OpenAI and SoftBank recently announced plans to build a new data center at the Lordstown site, which will be on one of the plant’s parking lots.
“He became a huge leader from that fight onward for the whole trade world,” Lori Wallach, who then led Public Citizen’s trade program, told me. A loose, bipartisan political coalition emerged, primarily to prevent the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) from being enacted. It spanned older New Deal Democrats, young labor-minded Democrats like Brown, and even far-right Republicans, an emerging political strain that attacked free trade from an economic-nationalist perspective, helping lay the groundwork for Trump’s rise. The coalition battled the establishment wings of both parties. But it failed to stop NAFTA; a majority of Republicans in the House voted for it, as did more than a hundred Democrats.
In the following years, Democrats increasingly came to be identified as the party of free trade, weakening the bond between organized labor and the Party that had been forged during the New Deal era. NAFTA’s enactment paved the way for the passage of another bill, which established permanent normal trade relations with China, facilitating its entry into the World Trade Organization (W.T.O.) in 2001 and accelerating the decline of manufacturing jobs in the United States. Despite the dissent of Brown and others, seventy-three House Democrats voted for this, too. Still, the number of defections was fewer than for NAFTA; Brown and others were moving the needle. Brown became the leader of the House Trade Working Group, a caucus of Democratic representatives opposed to free-trade agreements who whipped votes on those deals. Brown spearheaded the opposition to the Central America Free Trade Agreement, a deal with five Central American countries and the Dominican Republic pushed by President George W. Bush. The deal passed the House but with only fifteen Democrats voting for it. The following year, Brown was elected to the first of three Senate terms.
In the 2008 Presidential election, Barack Obama recognized the political salience of deindustrialization and wanted to tap into the coalition that Brown had helped create. At a primary debate in Cleveland, Obama admonished Hillary Clinton for her past support for NAFTA; he ran ads in Rust Belt states attacking John McCain for opposing Buy American provisions. In 2009, shortly after the auto bailout, President Obama and Brown visited the Lordstown plant to celebrate the arrival of the Cruze, the fuel-efficient model that G.M. would later discontinue. Yet throughout his Presidency, Obama largely continued Clinton’s embrace of free trade. He pushed for the Trans-Pacific Partnership, a sprawling trade deal, and never sought to renegotiate or withdraw from NAFTA, which was continuing to hollow out the Mahoning Valley. Around that time, Delphi, an auto-parts manufacturer, which had been shipping jobs to Mexico for years, closed a plant in the area that at times had employed as many as thirteen thousand people. “I think the people have become jaded there,” Green, now the U.A.W.’s regional director for Ohio and Indiana, said. He rattled off a litany of failed companies that had been promoted as the valley’s economic saviors. “They also remember and blame Bill Clinton and NAFTA for the enormous amount of job losses. There’s a lot of hard feelings around the Democrats, just because of NAFTA, that people never really got over, or weren’t able to express in an election cycle until Trump came along.”
In 2016, Trump’s campaign was able to co-opt much of what had made Brown electorally successful in a place like Ohio. Once he was in office, Trump renegotiated NAFTA, replacing it with the United States-Canada-Mexico Trade Agreement, which includes a pro-labor provision that allows the U.S. to investigate labor-rights violations in Mexico. (Brown was primarily responsible for that provision.) Brown and most Democrats voted for Trump’s deal, but it has done little to stanch the flow of jobs to Mexico. Ohio’s rightward movement continued, and by the 2018 midterms Brown was the only Ohio Democrat holding statewide office. Unsure how to survive the political headwinds, Brown appeared to tack toward the center. “I think it’s a terrible mistake if the Democratic nominee would publicly support Medicare for All,” he told CNN in 2019. By 2024, during his doomed reëlection campaign, he was running ads in which he wore a bulletproof vest and appeared with Border Patrol officers while boasting of his support “for the most conservative immigration bill in decades.” Then he decided to include Bill Clinton at his final campaign rally, confounding some observers, given the former President’s role in ushering in NAFTA and China’s admittance to the W.T.O. Brown lost to Moreno by four points.
Polls suggest that Brown has a slim lead in the race—a tight contest, given high inflation and Trump’s historic unpopularity, that perhaps reflects Husted’s effort to portray Brown as someone who has been in D.C. too long. (A recent poll showed that twenty-five per cent of Ohio’s likely voters thought Brown was still the incumbent.) Patricia Spencer, a retired lawyer who lived in the Mahoning Valley for decades, attended Brown’s rally with her husband. Spencer has been a Democrat since the fourth grade, and lamented how the valley’s economic collapse changed its political character. She is frustrated with the Democratic old guard; she and her husband expressed admiration for younger politicians such as Zohran Mamdani and Abdul El-Sayed. “It’s not just Sherrod; it’s all of them,” she said. “They weren’t effective. You may have had the right ideas, you might have had the right issues. But, for whatever reason, you were not effective. You did not stop this.” She went on, “I hope to God Sherrod wins, but what does that do for the future?”
The following day, I took a drive with Dan Adams, a sixty-one-year-old retired assembly-line worker, around the Lordstown plant, where he started as a temporary employee in 1989. When Adams began working at the plant, where his father and brother worked, too, G.M. offered three shifts per day, and the line never stopped. He became active in the union and was elected to Local 1112’s executive board. Over the years, Adams did a host of tricky, repetitive jobs—installing wiring harnesses in car doors as they moved down the line, drilling screws into instrument panels. (“That’s three thousand two hundred and twenty-eight screws a day,” he said, massaging his wrist. “You’re gonna get some tension in there.”) Then the plant shut down when he was seven years shy of the thirty he needed to collect his pension. He took a job at a Cadillac plant in Lansing, Michigan, while his wife and two children stayed behind. He drove back on weekends, except during the winter, when he took all the overtime he could get. Sometimes he worked seven days a week.
Like Adams, hundreds of other workers left the valley for good after the plant closed, taking their families with them, further diluting the presence of organized labor and hastening the area’s rightward political drift. In 2022, G.M., in partnership with Ultium, a South Korean company, and helped by billions in federal loans for green technology from the Biden Administration, opened a lithium-ion-battery plant on the old G.M. factory grounds. But the plant was nonunion; starting pay was sixteen dollars and fifty cents per hour. The union, and congressional allies such as Brown, pressured the Administration to insure that the new plants became unionized. They worried that the electric-vehicle market, boosted by government subsidies, would become a low-wage carve-out in auto manufacturing. “These workers feel betrayed because Presidents of both parties, from Bush to Clinton, then Bush 2, then Obama, then Trump, have sold them out,” Brown told the Times during the Ultium contract negotiations. “We keep pushing the White House to do more.”
By the end of the year, workers at the Ultium plant voted overwhelmingly to join the U.A.W., and wages for some of them have risen to more than forty-three dollars per hour. Adams was able to transfer back to Lordstown to finish out the remaining years required for his pension. But Trump’s termination of electric-vehicle tax credits, for both consumers and manufacturers, has devastated the plant. In January, nearly fourteen hundred workers, including Adams, were laid off. In August, he and several hundred others were called back, but some six hundred jobs were permanently eliminated. Last month, he worked his last shift, without fanfare. He never liked working in the battery plant—the safety gear and clean rooms made him feel confined, and he was frustrated by how unaware the younger workforce was of what the U.A.W. had done for them.
We drove to a gate where he used to punch in, and he pointed out his favorite parking spot. Nearby were stacks of metal piping and other construction materials for the data center that was now being built on the lot. Adams remains a loyal Democrat, and is grateful for Brown’s support of his union. “If we called Sherrod, he was there,” Adams said. “Never a staffer.” Still, Adams wondered whether Brown couldn’t have done “a little bit more” to fight the plant closure. “I wish that another generation had gotten a chance to go in there and say, ‘I’m gonna raise my family, I’ve got a good wage. I’ve got union protection,’ and the name Local 1112 stays alive.”
Despite its economic decline, the valley’s political importance has arguably grown. A few days after I met with Adams, Brown stopped at a bar in Youngstown, saying that he had visited the area every month for the past decade. “Who knows better than people in this valley how the system is being rigged?” he told the crowd. The week after, Trump returned to the site of his 2017 “Don’t move” rally, joined by Husted. Belying his long history as a Chamber of Commerce Republican, Husted ran through familiar tropes of right-wing populism, blaming Democrats exclusively for fifty years of the valley’s job losses. “They shipped their steel jobs overseas,” he said. “They shipped their auto jobs overseas.” He claimed that Trump had turned the valley “red forever.” Trump, in his speech, called Brown a “Dumocrat” who believes that “Christopher Columbus should not be in Columbus, Ohio.” Just then, members of the crowd assaulted a female protester in a shirt that read “Release the Epstein Files,” grabbing her hair and punching her in the face until police pulled her away. Trump called the woman a “paid protester,” “scum,” and “a fat guy.”
The speech, in which the President praised Husted’s “ass,” attacked Somali citizens, and venerated A.I. (“It’s not artificial anymore. It’s superintelligence . . . and everybody likes it”), also included a through-the-looking-glass celebration of Ohio’s economy. “After years of steel mills and factories closing across Ohio, our steel industry is roaring back to life,” he said. “Manufacturing is booming.” Neither Trump nor Husted mentioned the Ultium layoffs, or a truck plant near Dayton that had closed last month. The crowd was raucous, but it was hard to hide the fact that it was not even close to capacity. Attendance was reported to be less than half the size it had been nine years earlier, when Trump urged locals not to sell their homes. The empty seats reminded me of something Dan Adams had told me: “I think this election could be the beginning of the end of MAGA.” Adams added a warning to companies, along with politicians from both parties, about trying to sell false assurances of economic restoration. “There’s only so many times that this valley can raise their hand and say, ‘We got kicked in the balls again,’ ” he said. “If you’re not gonna keep your promises, don’t even fucking come around here.” ♦
news.summary: Sherrod Brown, who built his career as an avatar of blue-collar frustration, lost his Senate seat as more and more working-class voters defected to Trump. Now he is looking for a comeback.
news.author: Dan Kaufman

news.title: Dems hope to clinch the state by flipping Collin County, Paxton’s homebase and a longtime GOP bastion
news.text:
McKINNEY — For much of her life, Liz Slack voted Republican up and down the ballot.

A longtime resident of Collin County — the hometown of U.S. Senate nominee Ken Paxton — Slack said she looks like a typical conservative: a Baylor University alum who goes to Bible study every week.

But as the GOP became more hardline over the past decade, she felt her center-right values — which she said did not change — grow increasingly distant from the party she’d long supported. Slack stuck with Republicans in 2016 and 2018. But as the Trump era wore on, she began to evaluate her votes race-by-race, and ultimately cast ballots for the top two Democrats in 2024: Kamala Harris for president and Colin Allred for U.S. Senate. This fall, she’s planning to vote for James Talarico.

“It’s kind of funny, because in my mind, I don’t know that I’ve accepted that I’ve switched,” Slack said. “The other night at dinner, one friend was like, ‘You’re a Democrat now. Just accept it!’”

Slack is among a cohort of voters the GOP has struggled to retain in recent cycles — college-educated, suburban women. The party has been able to withstand the bleeding in Texas by picking up new cohorts, especially non-college educated voters of color. But as corporate relocations and booming growth make Texas’ suburbs larger and more diverse, the voting trends in places like McKinney are enormously consequential for both parties as they battle for control over a red state whose hue has become dangerously pale for Republicans this cycle.

Nowhere are the patterns of suburban growth and political transformation more on display than Collin County — where Paxton got his political start as a state representative in 2003 and eventually rose to serve as attorney general. While nearby Tarrant County has long been considered the Texas bellwether, statewide Democrats are bullish about their chances of winning there, as their candidates have in recent cycles. 

Instead, Talarico’s path to victory may require doing what no federal Democrat has done since 1970 when Lloyd Bentsen defeated George H.W. Bush in his first Senate run: win Collin County.

For Paxton, the results will be a testament to how the area has shifted as its most famous politician’s career has grown, with some of his most ardent supporters and passionate detractors having been along for the ride.

The dueling campaigns recognize the importance of the county too. Collin County is the most populous county in America that a statewide Democratic candidate has never won this century. Talarico kicked off his final statewide tour in Plano on the eve of early voting, one of several visits he’s made to the county this cycle. Paxton, meanwhile, was at a Tex-Mex restaurant in Allen on the first day of early voting, a town he hit in February, May and August.

“For 10 years, it’s been getting a little purpler,” said Shelby Williams, a former Collin County GOP chair and Plano City Council member now running for County Commission, who noted that Republicans spent years turning Collin County from blue to red decades ago. “If we can take it from them, they can take it right back from us. And we’re watching that unfold election cycle after election cycle, chipping away a little bit.”

Driving that political swing is massive growth and a more diverse population.

The county’s population has more than doubled since 2000, climbing to nearly 1.3 million. And it’s not slowing down any time soon. Four of the five fastest-growing cities in the nation are located in Collin County — Celina, Princeton, Melissa and Anna.

Over half of the population has at least a bachelor’s degree, and the median household income is $121,600 — second highest in the state.

Perhaps most importantly, Collin County has become one of the most diverse places in Texas — about 45% white, 23% Asian, 17% Hispanic and 12% Black. It is home to the state’s second largest Asian population, a group where Republicans have made significant gains in recent cycles. This year, however, anti-Indian rhetoric among GOP candidates has emerged as a flashpoint in the race, which could play a meaningful role as to whether the county swings blue.

“Collin County’s been moving towards a blue county for a while now, and that had a lot to do with our population growth,” said Jeremy Sutka, the Collin County Democratic Party chair. “There’s already a path that was heading there. What’s happening in 2026 is really a matter of whether or not we can accelerate that path.”

The politics of growth

Situated between downtown Dallas and the Red River, Collin County metamorphosed from a wheat and dairy farming community to a key part of the metro economy as the region boomed and suburbanized in the second half of the 20th century. 

By 2000, the county had nearly 500,000 residents and, like suburbs across the state, was firmly Republican. 

In the past quarter century alone, the county has continued to explode with growth. Through a combination of good schools, abundant housing and attracting the corporate headquarters of companies including FedEx, Frito Lay and Toyota North America, Collin County has transformed from a collection of commuter towns into an economic engine in its own right.

That growth has enabled Collin County’s shift from Republican stronghold to purple. For much of the 21st century, Collin County voted for the GOP at higher rates than the state as a whole did. But by the 2020 presidential campaign, Collin County crossed the rubicon, voting to the left of the state for the first time in decades, while still supporting Republican candidates. In 2018, when U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz won the state by less than 3 percentage points, he held Collin County by about 6 percentage points. 

Six years later, Cruz won his Senate race by a much larger 8-percentage point margin. But he only won Collin County by 5 percentage points.

Ross Hunt, a GOP operative in Dallas, said Collin County’s purpling has come from its economic opportunity, driving people to move there for jobs over ideology.

“Collin is sort of a dark horse county for the Democrats,” Hunt said. “Collin County used to be so red, and they’ve taken advantage of the fact that many of the immigrants into DFW have been motivated by economic factors.”

Republicans cautioned against solely blaming transplants for Collin County’s shift. 

Williams, the former Collin County GOP chair, pointed out that in 2018, exit polling showed that Democrat Beto O’Rourke won the native Texan vote, while Cruz won transplants en route to his narrow victory.

“Everybody blamed the people from California,” Williams said. “But if you looked at the data, it wasn’t the people from California. It was the natives that voted, for a variety of reasons. Some of the greatest patriots I’ve ever met are people who came from California, and they knew exactly why they left and where they were going.”

Even Paxton, whose father was in the Air Force, spent part of his childhood in California, before he would later move to Texas and eventually base his law practice in McKinney.

South Asian blowback

Democrats also believe the party is poised to make gains with the county’s significant Indian and Muslim American communities — though doing so could be an uphill battle. 

Texas Republicans have traditionally overperformed with South Asians relative to the bloc’s voter trends in the rest of the country. The GOP over several years has in particular made significant strides with Indian American voters, the most frequently Democratic group nationally among Asian American voters. Trump narrowly won several Asian-heavy precincts in Frisco in 2024, according to VoteHub, after a campaign in which the Collin County GOP hung Trump-Vance signs in Hindi, Telugu, Gujarati and Tamil. And the Texas GOP chairman from 2024 through earlier this year was Abraham George, an Indian American and a former Collin County GOP chair himself.

Polling from Asian Texans for Justice, a nonpartisan statewide organization working to build Asian political power, found that there has been a significant shift toward the GOP in Texas since 2022. Forty percent of Asian Texans identify as Republicans, according to the organization’s 2026 polling, while only 31% consider themselves Democrats — close to the inverse of where Asian Texan partisanship stood in 2022. 

But Collin County’s South Asian community has been at the center of a massive wave of hate from right-wing activists and influencers in places like Frisco, where city council meetings have become derailed by anti-Indian racism during public comment. Those sentiments have in many cases been echoed by GOP officials. Few, if any Texas Republicans, have explicitly condemned the recent wave of anti-Indian racism that has stemmed from policy concerns about H1-B visas.

Those tensions were inflamed in September, when, in the aftermath of an improbable University of Texas football win, Republican railroad commissioner nominee Bo French posted a photo of mostly South Asian students storming the field in Longhorn orange, writing “the problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.” The post fueled a political fire storm, causing multiple people from his own party to call for him to apologize — which he never did. 

Already, Sutka said, early voting data shows increased turnout in neighborhoods with significant Indian populations.

Nabila Mansoor, the Asian Texans for Justice executive director, said she expected heightened political activity in Collin County given the wave of anti-Indian hate — a trend that could resonate beyond 2026 as the community, like the county itself, continues to grow.

“It’s been really heartening to see how activated the community has [be]come, and then how how quickly the South Asian community got together to really fight against some of these forces that were infiltrating those communities and trying to prevent some of this racist rhetoric that you’re seeing come out of these places out in North Texas,” Mansoor said. “

Split-ticket voting

On a September block walk in Frisco with Brittany Black, a Democratic candidate for a Collin County statehouse district Trump won by 16 percentage points, the evidence of recent transplants was everywhere; window and car decals for non-Texas sports teams covered the neighborhood.

Black said corruption rose to be the district’s number two issue over the summer — a trend that has inspired her to tie Paxton, who was impeached by the Texas House over bribery allegations and ultimately acquitted by the Texas Senate, into her discussion of her race as much as possible. She thinks the top of the ticket frustration with Paxton in his home county can trickle down the ballot.

“I’ve heard a lot more people than ever saying that they’re just not going to vote,” Black said. “They’re just like, I can’t bring myself to vote for a Democrat, but I can’t vote for this guy either.”

That attitude could contribute to significant levels of split ticket voting — a phenomenon that could end up keeping downballot Republicans safe. Sutka said, for example, he drove by a house in downtown McKinney that had yard signs for both Talarico and Republican county clerk Stacey Kemp.

Anne Bramlett, a senior in Lavon, is one such longtime Collin County voter who has moved away from the GOP. Bramlett considers herself a lifelong Republican, but has not voted straight ticket in years over frustrations with the GOP’s stance on Medicaid funding, a critical lifeline for her adult son with autism who lives in a Medicaid waiver group home. She plans to vote for Talarico for Senate and Democratic governor nominee Gina Hinojosa, but also her local Republican state representative, Candy Noble. Further down the ballot, she was still deciding.

“Locally, I’ve always voted for the Republicans in the commissioners’ court and judge [races],” Bramlett said. “But I’m kind of straying away from that too. I’m just looking carefully at what they say and what they believe.”

Her husband, Bramlett said, is a Republican and Trump voter who is torn over the U.S. Senate race. He won’t vote for Talarico given the Democrat’s positions on social issues like abortion. But he is concerned about the allegations of corruption and infidelity surrounding Paxton, Bramlett said, and he might skip the race altogether.

news.title: LIZ PEEK: Five reasons Republicans could defy the polls and shock Democrats on Election Day
news.text: Election Day is one week away. Most pundits are ready to declare the midterms over and Democrats the victors. But hold on: There are several reasons Republicans may outperform the gloomy polls and forecasts making headlines. First, Democrats are unpopular. A recent CNN poll showed Democratic favorability at 35%, considerably below the 38% awarded President Trump in the most recent RealClearPolling average. Second, Republicans are flush with campaign cash that is now flowing into tough races across the country. Money doesn’t win elections (see: Kamala Harris), but it can help snag undecided voters. That is true especially in contests like the Michigan Senate race, where little-known Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is facing off against Mike Rogers, a veteran and moderate GOP former congressman. Voters are just now discovering allegations about El-Sayed’s possible family ties to the designated terrorist group, the Muslim Brotherhood, causing the polls to tighten. Fox News recently reported, "El-Sayed has also faced scrutiny over social media posts from his half-sister describing their mother's alleged involvement in Muslim Brotherhood activism in the 1970s. He has denied personal or family ties to the organization and said he was raised by his father and stepmother." ABDUL EL-SAYED'S ALLEGED FAMILY TIES TO MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD SURFACE AFTER DENYING ANY LINK DURING NBC INTERVIEW Third, President Trump is campaigning vigorously, reminding voters why they elected him. Given the incessant attacks on the commander in chief by the liberal media, his rallies are essential. Yes, his approval numbers have been weighed down by the Iran war, but his appearances will help drive turnout. Fourth, the far left overwhelmed primaries earlier this year, causing Democrats to put up some controversial candidates, like Senate hopefuls James Talarico in Texas and Troy Jackson in Maine. LIZ PEEK: A BLUE WAVE? THE LIBERAL MEDIA WANTS ONE, BUT VOTERS MIGHT DISAGREE Fifth, to quote a recent piece in The Economist: "The polls could be wrong." While the publication concludes that polling errors at the national level have, in different elections, overcounted both Republicans and Democrats, when it comes to specific states and districts, the goofs follow "a remarkably consistent pattern." In the current races, The Economist writes, "applying the historical trend to this year’s polls reverses Democratic leads in the pivotal states of Alaska and Texas. In Ohio, the Democratic advantage would be cut to less than one percentage point, while Iowa and Kansas would move from being tied to leaning Republican." LEE CARTER: POLLS SAY DEMOCRATS COULD SWAMP REPUBLICANS. AS A POLLSTER, I HAVE A QUESTION CNN reported the same thing a few nights ago, with analyst Harry Enten describing Democrats’ lead in numerous toss-up states as "nominal" and pointing out that polling in states won by Trump in the past has undercounted Republicans by more than 4 points. If that same level of error persists, the GOP will win in Texas, Maine, Iowa and Kansas, and keep the Senate. In this year’s election cycle, polling has come under even more scrutiny than usual, especially as totally made-up surveys have entered the mix and been included in supposedly sophisticated aggregates like those published by The New York Times and FiftyPlusOne, which helped reveal the frauds. An outfit called Wedgewood Polls admitted that it had fabricated polls as an "experiment." Some have alleged the fake surveys were meant to boost far-left candidates like Wisconsin gubernatorial hopeful Francesca Hong, while others have insinuated that the originators of the Wedgewood polls were using betting sites to benefit from the fallout. DEMOCRATS FURIOUS AFTER POLLSTER BOOSTING FAR-LEFT CANDIDATES ADMITS FABRICATING SURVEYS: ‘ABSOLUTE SCUMBAGS’ Wedgewood isn’t alone; several other survey organizations, including Median Strategies and Public Sentiment Institute, have also been revealed as dishonest or out-and-out frauds. Whatever confidence people had in the polling industry has deflated like a Hillary Clinton election-night balloon. Remember that most media outlets are rooting for Democrats to take over Congress and punish President Trump. Publishing stories and polls that present the election as essentially over is calculated. If it suppresses GOP turnout and campaign donations in close races, so much the better. DEMOCRATS THINK A BLUE WAVE IS BUILDING. HERE ARE 3 FORCES THAT COULD STOP IT No one should be driven by polls or gloomy headlines. Instead, consider which candidate is offering policies that history shows lead to better outcomes: lower taxes, lighter regulations that reduce costs, robust law enforcement that produces safer communities, strict oversight of welfare spending that reduces fraud and enables assistance for those who need it, and rigorous education. Those are the policies that have made Florida more successful than New York and Texas more appealing than California. Policies matter. OBAMA PREPARES TO RALLY WITH MICHIGAN DEM WHO ONCE DELIVERED SCATHING VERDICT ON HIS PRESIDENCY Voters should also ignore Democratic race-baiting. When President Obama, campaigning in Michigan with Sen. Elissa Slotkin for Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, said, "Imagine the power duo of Abdul and Elissa. You got a Muslim man, a Jewish woman, fighting for you in the U.S. Senate. That’s something, Michigan, you can be proud of." That’s vintage Obama, slicing and dicing our politics along race and gender lines, which should have nothing to do with how you vote. What does matter — in Michigan as elsewhere — is that progressives like El-Sayed are pushing Medicare for All and want to eliminate the kind of gold-plated private insurance packages that unions like the UAW have worked so hard to win. El-Sayed claims that if you like your existing insurance, you can keep it, reminding us of President Obama’s false promise that "If you like your healthcare plan, you can keep it." That canard was PolitiFact’s Lie of the Year in 2013 after Obamacare caused millions of plans to be canceled. You cannot provide free healthcare, free childcare and free services to people in the U.S. illegally without boosting taxes. New York is already the most-taxed state in the country. The budget for the state is twice that of Florida despite having fewer residents; this is unsustainable. What matters across the country is maintaining U.S. energy self-sufficiency and boosting employment. When New York progressive Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez calls to shut down fossil fuel production and Gov. Kathy Hochul slaps a moratorium on new hyperscale data centers, they are embracing policies that will cost their state jobs and incomes. That matters. news.title: MORNING GLORY: The Democrats have a 'Fanatic Four' of extremist Senate candidates
news.text: Despite the basic rule of politics — it takes 50% of the vote plus one to win — both parties have occasionally put forward nominees from the farther reaches of the right or from the extreme left. Those candidates have sometimes combined terrible public personalities and debate skills with policy positions far beyond the edges of mainstream politics. This year Democrats are trying to sell four extremists to voters: Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota, Troy Jackson in Maine and James Talarico in Texas. In three of those four races, Republicans have countered with nominees from the center: Mike Rogers in Michigan, Michele Tafoya in Minnesota and the incumbent in Maine, Senator Susan Collins, who, as Chair of the Senate Committee on Appropriations is the most powerful woman inside the Beltway and whose defeat would be an enormous "own goal" for Mainers. MORNING GLORY: FIVE SENATE RACES SHOW WHY DEMOCRATS MAY REGRET THEIR PRIMARY CHOICES The Republican Senate nominee in Texas is the state’s own attorney general, Ken Paxton, who has run and won three times in the Lone Star State. Paxton is a flawed candidate, but he will be a reliable GOP vote in the Senate and the party has rallied to him even though there are bruised feelings from the contentious primary. Republicans have indulged their base over the years, especially in 2010 when it put forward Christine O’Donnell in Delaware, Sharron Angle in Nevada, and Ken Buck in Colorado, and in 2012 with the nominations of Todd Akin in Missouri and Richard Mourdock in Indiana. All five of those Republicans lost. This year, a week out from Election Day, it especially doesn’t look good for Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Troy Jackson in Maine. El-Sayed has a reflexive attitude of grievance and in Maine, Jackson suffers in any side-by-side comparison with Susan Collins, who is a formidable political athlete. DAVID MARCUS: IN BLUE MAINE, NOBODY BELIEVES SUSAN COLLINS WILL LOSE UNTIL THEY SEE IT Talarico has seen Paxton rise and rise in the polls and the GOP has spent millions showing Texans how far out in left field Talarico plays. Talarico weirdly vanished from the campaign trail for a dozen days and blamed the flu. In Minnesota — the "bluest" of the four states, the epic fraud scandal has followed Flanagan's campaign, who has been the state’s Lieutenant Governor since 2019. Flanagan is matched against the political "rookie of the year" in Republican moderate Michele Tafoya, a sparkling and affable centrist. Democrats have tried to prop up their failing four fanatics by sending out Bernie Sanders, Alexandria Ocasio Cortez, former Vice President Kamala Harris and have pulled former President Barack Obama off Martha’s Island to throw him into the breach. Trouble is "AOC," "Bernie," and "Kamala" all telegraph "whacky or worse" into the electorate’s consciousness, and the former president’s schtick was old in 2014 when he helped provoke a red wave with Republicans netting nine Senate seats and a baker’s dozen House seats. EL-SAYED’S SCATHING OBAMA CRITIQUE RESURFACES AHEAD OF JOINT CAMPAIGN RALLY El-Sayed’s campaign seems to be in free-fall as the candidate first turned argumentative, then angry, in appearances culminating last week with his interview with Fox News’ own Bret Baier. El-Sayed’s hostile and rude treatment of Baier — the quintessential gentleman of the news business — was instantly understood by anyone who saw it as an attempt to hide his record by loudly talking over Baier’s questions and deflecting to non-issues unrelated to Baier’s straightforward and brief questions. That interview may have done the candidate the most damage of the cycle as it came after Rogers had just blistered El-Sayed in their final debate. El-Sayed’s many attempts in many settings to cover up the details of his "Medicare for All" tax-spend-and-ration health care boondoggle with semantics and word puzzles left viewers wondering on what topic could they actually trust El-Sayed? Certainly not Iran or Islamist extremism, as El-Sayed’s frantic attempts to escape his past actions and statements have backfired. El-Sayed’s biggest blunder — his declaration that "hurt people hurt people" after an attack on a Michigan synagogue — has never receded in the public’s mind. Rogers, meanwhile, has methodically campaigned in traditional Democratic strongholds in and around Detroit and Pontiac and stresses his distinguished career as a federal and state legislator, FBI agent and Army officer. DAVID MARCUS: THE 5 FACTORS THAT COULD DECIDE MICHIGAN'S TIGHT AND UGLY SENATE RACE Peggy Flanagan and James Talarico simply haven’t, and apparently cannot, connect with the center of their states’ electorates. They are just "way outside the ‘40s’" where most of American politics, like most NFL games, are played. Flanagan’s campaign is mired in the swamp of the massive fraud that engulfed part of the Twin Cities’ Somali community. Talarico’s long tenure among "the woke" has haunted him throughout the campaign, as has his resting face of innocent cluelessness. DEMOCRATS WHO ‘NEVER VOTED REPUBLICAN’ BACK ROGERS OVER EL-SAYED IN RAZOR-CLOSE RACE Up in Maine, Troy Jackson got waxed by the veteran Collins in four out of four debates in all of which Jackson struggled with very basic questions about very basic issues — like the enormous difference between Medicare and Medicaid. "Oh shut up!" Jackson also grunted into a microphone on the debate stage as Collins made a joke about a debate disrupter being a Jackson supporter. Mainers are a polite lot. They also know that turning out the Chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee in favor of a guy who often looks like he slept outside and just woke up would be a singularly unwise trade for everyone in the state. When the Democratic Socialists of America’s ("DSA") hand-picked erratic and voluble Graham Platner had to exit the Maine race, the Maine Democratic Party could have picked anyone in the state to replace him. That they chose Jackson, the third place loser from the then just-completed Democratic gubernatorial primary, remains one of the baffling questions in a year of political surprises. The GOP is "coming home" as President Donald Trump has exhausted his own team with daily rallies and sometimes two. The cliché that "it all comes down to turnout" isn’t lost on the president who knows the hatred of the left is priced into his persona, but that getting his own voters to the polls is exactly what his rallies do. Republicans learned from their "Tea Party" years that candidates cannot win with their bases, but also that you can’t win with just the base. news.title: Susan Collins vs. Troy Jackson on AI Data Centers Amid Maine Voters' Fears
news.text: Senator Susan Collins and her Democratic challenger Troy Jackson have both embraced calls for guardrails on data centers ahead of the Maine Senate race, as polling finds that Maine voters are skeptical of their construction in the Pine Tree State. The midterm elections have been defined by the debate over artificial intelligence (AI) powered data centers, as a growing number of Americans—and Mainers—say they do not want to see them built in their communities. Collins has generally walked a fine line on data centers, voting for the Ratepayer Protection Act and calling for more local control over the issue. Meanwhile, Jackson has been highly critical of data center developers and has called for the state to implement a moratorium on their construction. The issue could be impactful in the race, which is one of a handful of toss-ups that could determine whether Democrats or Republicans control the Senate after the midterms. Proponents of data centers believe they are an important economic lifeline for communities that have the potential to create jobs. Critics, however, have raised numerous issues with data centers, including their impact on the environment, water usage, their potential to drive up electricity bills and noise pollution. In Maine, a state with a culture that values conservation, several municipalities have implemented moratoriums on data centers, as they are “very unpopular” in the state, Mark Brewer, professor of political science at the University of Maine in Orono, told Newsweek. “An exception might be old mill towns that have lost their mill but still have much of the infrastructure in place,” he added. The data center debate was on display during a viral moment in the final debate between the two candidates when a data center protester briefly disrupted while Collins was speaking. Collins said the protester was “obviously one of Troy’s supporters,” to which Jackson responded, “Oh, shut up. I don’t even know that kid.” During an October 13 debate, Collins said that the two candidates are “not that far apart on this particular issue” during a discussion about data centers. Here is a look at where the two candidates stand on the matter. Susan Collins Position on Data Centers Collins touted her support for the Ratepayer Protection Act, which required states to consider establishing standards for when data centers and other large electricity users connect to the grid, during the debate. “I voted and cosponsored a bill that the Senate considered just last month to put guardrails and encourage states to adopt guardrails on the construction of data centers. That included making sure that they have no impact on electric rates, very important for a state like Maine with the fourth highest electric rates in the country due to Troy’s policies,” she said. The senator said she believes the issue is decided locally. “There may be a former mill site, as Governor [Janet] Mills has said, where a data center would work out all right because there is a source of power and water, but in many other places, they would not work well,” she said. A spokesperson for Collins pointed to her statement about the Ratepayer Protection Act when reached by Newsweek. “Maine families and small businesses are already paying some of the highest electricity costs in the nation,” Collins said. “The bipartisan Ratepayer Protection Act ensures that they will not pay an even steeper bill by directing state utility regulators to consider standards that would make high-volume users like AI data centers offset their own costs. Mainers should not have to pay the bill for data centers’ power generation, transmission lines, and energy infrastructure.” Newsweek’s AI scorecard rates Collins as “Leans AI Skeptic.” Troy Jackson's Position on Data Centers Jackson has been much more critical of data centers. During the October 13 debate, Jackson said data centers have the ability to “create some jobs,” but that data centers being built in Maine cannot increase electricity rates or hurt the state’s water quality. “I want to make sure that we know what the data is. How they are using it, and there has to be real parameters, real guidelines to how we’re going to do this,” Jackson said. “I’m not really supportive of data centers, but I understand they’re maybe something that we have to deal with.” Jackson said data centers must be slowed down so people can better understand their development. “I am very much in favor of making sure the federal government or the state of Maine puts guardrails on these things because I don’t want the billionaires, again, writing the rules and making our communities worse off than they are right now,” he said. While campaigning for governor earlier this year, Jackson criticized Mills for vetoing a moratorium on data center development in the state. “Once again, we’re seeing power and influence coming into this state and ruining things for us Mainers. We needed a pause on this because it takes our power. It takes our water. There’s health effects. We need regulations because we don’t know what they’re doing without data, our information. We don’t know all the health effects to our kids,” he said. Newsweek reached out to Jackson's campaign via email. How Maine Voters View Data Centers Data centers are unpopular in Maine, according to polls. Only 29 percent of Mainers support the construction of data centers in the U.S., compared to 66 percent of whom oppose their development, according to a poll from The New York Times and Siena University of 619 voters from September 15 to 22. Forty-one percent of respondents said they believed Jackson would do a better job on data centers, compared to 39 percent who said they trusted Collins more on the issue, according to the poll, which had a margin of error of plus or minus 5.4 percentage points. Several towns across the state, including Bangor, Brunswick, Sanford, Scarborough and Westbrook have implemented data center moratoriums, even as Mills vetoed legislation that would establish statewide limits earlier this year. Earlier this month, voters in Buxton, a small town outside of Portland, approved a moratorium. Portland, the state’s largest city, has not implemented a data center moratorium. Susan Collins vs. Troy Jackson: Maine Senate Polls, Odds Polling has shown a tight race in a state that backed former Vice President Kamala Harris by about 7 points in the 2024 election. Although Maine has a Democratic lean, Collins has been able to win in the past due to her personal popularity and image as one of the chamber's most bipartisan members. But Democrats are hopeful a national environment fueled by President Donald Trump's declining national approval rating could give Jackson a chance at unseating the longtime incumbent. A Suffolk University poll gave Jackson a 2-point lead, 49 percent to 47 percent. It surveyed 500 Maine voters October 8-11 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.4 percentage points. Collins also trailed by 2 points in an InsiderAdvantage survey of 1,200 likely voters from October 13 to 14. Jackson’s support stood at 49 percent to 47 percent for Collins. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.83 percentage points. Jackson was up 4 points among 800 likely voters in a poll from The Washington Post and George Mason University, conducted from September 30 to October 5. Fifty percent said they planned to vote for Jackson, compared with 46 percent for Collins. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.6 percentage points. Polls underestimated Collins in her 2020 reelection bid. She trailed Democrat Sara Gideon in public surveys but won with more than 50 percent of the vote. Forecasters like the Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball classified the race as a toss-up. Jackson had an edge in prediction markets as of Monday, when his chances of victory stood at 60 percent on Kalshi and 59 percent on Polymarket. Prediction markets allow traders to buy and sell contracts tied to political outcomes and current events, aggregating real‑money wagers into probability estimates. Prices fluctuate as traders react to polling, fundraising, candidate developments and broader political trends. They measure trader sentiment at a given moment but do not always accurately predict the future. Maine Voting: What to Know In-person absentee voting began on October 5 and will continue until October 29. Polling locations are open between 6 a.m. or 10 a.m. to 8 p.m., depending on a town’s population. As of October 26, 251,036 absentee ballots had been requested and 197,104 had been returned and accepted, according to data from the Maine Secretary of State office. news.summary: Collins and Jackson have debated their positions on data centers ahead of the Maine Senate race, a critical battleground.

news.title: As Election Day Nears, a Key House Race Remains in Flux
news.text:
NY-17: Fourth in a series on the environmental stakes behind one of the nation’s most fiercely contested congressional races.

After the Democratic primary election in New York’s hotly contested 17th Congressional District this June, William Knox, a veteran and self-described “anti-MAGA Republican,” said he was impressed by the winning candidate, a combat veteran who deployed six times in Iraq and Afghanistan and later served on the National Security Council in the Biden administration. 

 “I am willing to cross party lines and vote for Cait Conley,” Knox, a resident of Dutchess County, said at the time. 

Now, nine days away from the midterm elections, Knox is less convinced Conley is as qualified as he had initially hoped. 

“I’m on the fence again,” he said.

For many voters, the election has become a referendum on President Donald Trump, whose approval rating stands at around 33 percent. A recent NBC News poll found that more voters than at any point in three decades viewed their vote as a way to signal opposition to the president. 

Though still committed to curbing Donald Trump’s power, Knox is no longer convinced that voting for Mike Lawler, the Republican incumbent, necessarily amounts to voting for Trump.

“Mike seems to recognise that Trump’s coattails aren’t what they once were, and will be open to not voting the way Trump wants him to,” Knox said. 

In this district, one of 21 races rated as toss-ups by the Cook Political Report, and one of only three represented by a Republican seeking re-election in a district Kamala Harris carried in 2024, winning over voters like Knox will prove key. As the campaigns have gathered steam, some voters have firmed up their views, while others have begun to waver.

Democrats need to win just four of the 21 toss-up races to secure a majority, assuming they also hold the seats rated as leaning or likely Democratic. Republicans, meanwhile, would need to win 18, in addition to the seats that lean in their favour.

Their final televised debate in mid-October saw Lawler and Conley double down on their campaign messages, again trading barbs over their records and allegiances.

Artificial intelligence and data centers were the first subjects raised, reflecting their prominence in the race.

Jordan Turner, a voter from Rockland County who has followed both campaigns closely and remains firmly in Conley’s camp, said concerns over data centers extended beyond Orangeburg, a data center hotspot in the district that hosts five such facilities.

“It has become a national story,” he said. “When people see there’s a data center going up in Orangeburg, they go, ‘Oh my god, could there be a data center in Suffern or Katonah?’ They worry that everyone is going to be putting a data center on every corner.”

Recent polls suggest Americans’ views of data centers have grown more negative, with some finding that roughly two-thirds oppose new facilities in their communities. The issue has emerged as a rare point of convergence across the political divide.

Conley attacked Lawler’s support for President Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act and his ties to wealthy donors. She called him “Elon Musk’s guy,” pointing to more than $1.7 million in contributions Musk made to Lawler’s 2024 campaign, which exceeded those of any other House member.

Lawler turned the accusation back on his opponent. He again called into question her financial ties to the industry, including $328,000 from Hidden Level and Primer AI, which she explained as defense contracts for drone detection systems.

“She is the AI candidate for the AI industry,” he said. “She is not paying taxes here, and wants to do the bidding of AI.” 

Conley, who grew up in the Hudson Valley, moved from Virginia to the district last year.

Lawler defended local control over development and expressed support for local data-center moratoriums in Orangeburg and Fishkill, while arguing that Gov. Kathy Hochul’s statewide moratorium was not the answer. Conley, meanwhile, supports the moratorium but is not opposed to data centers outright, provided they are properly zoned and deliver a net benefit to the communities where they are built.

With gas prices up 43 percent since the war in Iran began, and diesel prices up 68 percent, energy affordability was also a central debate issue.

To lower energy prices, Lawler has advocated for the reopening of Indian Point, a nuclear power plant in the district that was shut down in 2021 and is presently being decommissioned. He has also called for permitting reform to boost domestic oil and gas production, including more extraction in the Southern Tier and expanded pipeline infrastructure.

When the U.S. Department of Energy recently announced to $42 million in Defense Production Act funding for the proposed 125-mile Constitution Pipeline, which would carry natural gas from Pennsylvania to New York, Lawler joined Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum at a gas-fired power plant in New York’s 18th Congressional District. 

He has consistently argued that Conley’s plans to phase out fossil fuels would leave consumers facing higher bills.

For Knox, energy costs are “top of mind.”

“My electricity bill has jumped precipitously. Nuclear is one of the most environmentally friendly ways we can get energy. I would have been happier if I had seen Cait Conley acknowledge that stopping the decommissioning of Indian Point would be a good thing for the district.”

Courtney Williams, a voter from Westchester County, welcomed some focus on environmental issues, including Indian Point and energy prices, but wished to hear more substantive proposals.

“I have warmed to Conley, but not so much on environmental issues,” she said. “There still isn’t a meaty plan for addressing existing problems in the absence of a functioning federal government or Environmental Protection Agency.”

Turner, meanwhile, didn’t see Indian Point as a major issue in the district. He worries that any low-information voters in the district, who see politics as a “dirty word”, may be convinced by Lawler’s bipartisan messaging. 

“Lawler has painted himself as a moderate,” he said. “He has convinced enough people that he’s charming and bipartisan. Yes, he is charming. He is not bipartisan.”

President Trump’s Republican Midterm Convention in Dallas in September saw some Republicans stay away. The New York Times reported that Ken Paxton, one of the Republican Party’s leading Senate candidates in Texas, said “everybody’s numbers dropped” after the convention.

Turner said Lawler’s attendance had attracted little attention locally. “Him being there got almost no press. I didn’t see anything about it here. Nobody cared.”

Knox had not known Lawler attended the convention. Learning of it, he said, would influence his vote.

“I’m torn,” he said. “It does influence my vote to know that he went to a Trump rally, and others didn’t. I would have liked it if he hadn’t.”

Lawler has sought to portray Conley as insufficiently bipartisan by tying her to New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-New York, both progressive Democratic Socialists. Turner questioned whether the attack still resonated with voters.

“Mamdani’s not such a boogeyman anymore,” he said. “People are going into New York City and going, ‘Where’s the hellhole we were promised?’”

Environmentalists in the district largely remain behind Conley. Peggy Kurtz, a voter from Rockland County who frequently campaigns in Haverstraw, a largely Latino community, said residents there had expressed dissatisfaction with the direction of the country under Trump.

“People are agreeing,” she said. “Will they come out to vote? I don’t know.”

With the election drawing closer, uncertainty remains. Some voters remain undecided about who will win their support; others are unsure which way the district will swing.
news.summary: NY-17: Fourth in a series on the environmental stakes behind one of the nation’s most fiercely contested congressional races. After the Democratic primary election in New York’s hotly contested 17th Congressional District this June, William Knox, a veteran and self-described “anti-MAGA Republican,” said he was impressed by the winning candidate, a combat veteran who deployed […]
